Name: David Seidman
Question: Why don’t tech companies or data scientist companies have training classes to lead into hiring?
Answer: The ROI isn't there. If you are really good at computers, there's a good chance you'll wind up in the field anyway, even if you have to take out a bunch of loans to do it. The salaries earned by engineers at big tech companies can easily pay off student loans in just a few years. Talented folks who don't go to school can work their way up at other jobs. For the company, there's no need to pay to reason people who would otherwise pay to train themselves. The people who might benefit from a training program are those who lack the confidence or aptitude to make it on their own. Obviously a company doesn't want to train those who have no aptitude. So that means the only people who would pay back the company's investment are those who have aptitude but not confidence. It's really hard to identify these people and distinguish them from those without aptitude and those who would pay for their own training. On top of that, if a company does successfully train someone, that person can quit and take those skills to a competitor. The company can put provisions in place to mitigate that, like requiring the person to pay back the training costs if they leave too quickly. But it's hard to make those provisions tight enough to be useful without being so tight as to be unpalatable or even illegal. That said, companies do have some training programs. These are often targeted at specific demographics that the company believes are likely to have aptitude but not confidence. There are some obvious reasons why people lack confidence: precarious financial situations, poor secondary education, and discrimination, among others. Companies try to target these groups for training. But the programs are usually pretty limited for the reasons given above.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Elon Musk is making liberals' heads explode while he gets rid of lazy employees and keeps only the best ones, those willing to work hard towards his vision. Will liberals try to break up Twitter when his strategy makes them hugely profitable?
Answer: Elon Musk isn't making liberals heads explode. Quite the opposite: most liberals I know are really enjoying this spectacle. An egotistical billionaire is losing lots of money, and conservatives will have to stop complaining about social media companies' liberal bias. I think a lot of liberals also expect that allowing uncensored free speech on Twitter will let a lot more noxious extreme right wing personalities get air time and it'll be a bad look for conservatives in general. It's very unlikely that the 30% of Twitter employees who are left are the best of them. First, in the initial 50% purge, entire functions like PR were cut completely. The #1 best PR person is gone. The same is true of many other teams. Second, Twitter probably did shed a bunch of dead weight in that 50%, but with managers given no time to prepare and none of the usual oversight, it's certain that many good people were let go due to bad manager assessments, politics, and even overt bias. Twitter is being sued over the latter. Third, consider the roughly 2000 people who quit when Musk required them to sign a loyalty and hard work pledge. Who do you think is more likely to snap quit like that: a top performer with a great reputation who can get a job anywhere overnight or a low performer? It's probably mostly low performers who are left. Fourth, even lazy, mediocre engineers can be critically important to the business if they have specialized knowledge. Engineers are not fungible. If there's only one person who really understands how a particular piece of code works, which is true more often than not, then firing that person without a planned transition is a disaster. So even if Musk could magically fire the worst 50% of employees, it would still be a huge disaster for the company. All that said, if Twitter somehow succeeds, I think we would see calls for more regulation, which there already are, but nothing significant would actually materialize, as it has not so far. No one has yet suggested any regulation that would be meaningful yet palatable to a Congressional majority. This show is going to play out in the free market.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Elon Musk correct in reportedly saying that engineering managers should spend their time coding?
Answer: I think it's ideal for engineering managers to spend about 10% of their time coding. The purpose is not to generate useful code but rather to ensure the manager is familiar with the team's technology and code base. If a team member proposes changing a technical dependency or refactoring the code, a manager who has done some hands on engineering will have a better sense of whether the proposal is a good one. The manager will also have a better sense of how different team members have contributed to the code base, which helps with performance reviews. However, this is only really feasible up to about 6 or 7 direct reports. Once a manager has more than that, they generally don't have enough spare time to keep coding. I kept coding until I had 8 direct reports. It might be reasonable for a company to require managers to code a bit as a demonstration of proficiency, as long as most managers have 8 or fewer reports. It would be pretty dumb to require managers to make meaningful code contributions, except at the very smallest companies. If you want more development work to get done, hire more developers. And expecting a manager to deal with 8+ direct reports while still adding features in code is going to lead to crappy code, crappy management, or most likely both. It's not just that time is limited, but also people are more effective at their jobs when they're able to specialize.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Elon Musk fired 50 percent of their colleagues, he has now cancelled remote work for them, and he is also now giving them impossible deadlines. Why are the remaining Twitter employees staying back? Don't they have any self respect?
Answer: The people who survived the initial purge have no particular urgency to leave. There are reports of people who were trying to quit and couldn't even find someone to take their resignation. If nobody in HR is available to process such a simple matter, it's highly unlikely that there's much time to process individual involuntary terminations for cause aka firings, which are much more complex. I also can't see managers being very aggressive about pushing the remaining 50% of their team out the door, especially since the lowest performers were probably already let go. So that means everyone who's left can get away with doing relatively little work while they work on their job hunt on a relaxed schedule. Or not even. I'm sure there are people just collecting a paycheck and planning to quit when someone actually bothers to try to fire them. It's not like anyone is going to care about references from Twitter at this point. If anything, having Twitter on your resume after 2022 may be a bit of a yellow flag. That's because of another set of people who are left: those who can't get another job because they are not very competent, not very nice or not very experienced. Hiring managers are going to ask the same question posed here: why did you stay? It's easy to rule out people who were too early in their career to leave easily, but those who are left will be suspect. Yet another group of people are those in the US on visas that are tied to their employer, who can't easily change jobs. They are pretty screwed. There are presumably also some employees who like Musk's approach and/or him personally. That itself will be somewhat of a yellow flag if Twitter continues what seems to be a death spiral. This is not intended as a comment on Musk personally, but if he runs the company into the ground, people who still stick with him as he does so are displaying some questionable business judgement. Of course, if he turns things around, the true believers will be rewarded both directly and in reputation. For what it's worth, Tesla and SpaceX are generally considered to hire good people (and to burn them out quickly, but, hey, you get to work on rockets).

Name: David Seidman
Question: How many L9s are there in Google?
Answer: Quite a few — I'd estimate hundreds. Level 9 is Senior Director, although in my experience they often don't use the “Senior” in practice. A Senior Director might have about 150–200 people in their org. So if there are about 30k engineers, there are about 200 Senior Directors to manage them all, plus about 40 VPs to manage them, and 10ish SVPs. Those numbers seem low to me, so there may be even more. There are also individual contributors (ICs) at L9 and higher, although very few of them. There might be one or two in a 1000 person org. This answer is based on engineering. I'm not sure about other roles. If they are similar, then there are probably a thousand or more people at L9+.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do you think tech companies should have immunity over problematic user content?
Answer: Yes, because the alternatives are even worse. I'll assume that “problematic content" refers to things that are considered undesirable but not actually illegal. I don't think anyone except the most extreme libertarians is arguing that tech companies should be allowed to knowingly host child sexual abuse imagery or death threats. We're talking here about misinformation, hate speech, toxic behavior, and things like that. If we were to take away platform immunity, we'd have to replace it with some standard for what's acceptable. The is zero consensus on what that standard would be. Is it undesirable hate speech to refer to a trans woman as a man, or is it political speech that should be protected? Under what circumstances should the word “queer" be allowed? How should we judge jokes? Who decides what is misinformation? And what should the penalty be for breaking the rules? These are hard questions to answer, and there's no set of answers that pleases everyone — not even close. Also, that standard would have to be administered by the government, which would cause a lot of problems. Any controversial regulatory decision might well be reversed after the next election, even retroactively. Your party loses an election so you get banned from Twitter for something you said a decade ago. Regulation and laws always change slowly and would inevitably fall far behind the current state of technology. Perhaps most important, we'd all be stuck with a single standard. Today, if you don't like Facebook's content moderation policies, you can use Truth. If enough people feel that way, Truth will take Facebook's business away. If Twitter's content policies are sufficiently out of line with what users want, it will get bought out by someone who will change those policies. But if the government set standards for what is and isn't allowed, we wouldn't have those options. So even though today's social media platforms have serious problems, replacing their immunity with an externally defined standard would be even worse.

Name: David Seidman
Question: "When do you consider code finished?" - Got this as a job interview question and didn't get the job.
Answer: Code is done when it meets the requirements. The requirements may or may not include features, stability, security, usability, maintainability, supportability, and legality. They may or may not be written down. You may have to spend a lot of time figuring out what “done" really is. And you're only ever done for the current release. As long as the product isn't cancelled, such as by bankruptcy, there will always be another version with new requirements. On a whiteboard at a company I used to work for, someone had written, “Software is never done, it just ships from time to time.” Their code really wasn't done, by any reasonable engineering standard, but they shipped it anyway and they stayed in business, so it must have been good enough. Sometimes the requirements can be really low.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do Google employees work long hours?
Answer: Rarely. In my experience, most Googlers worked about 40–45 hours/week, with some longer and shorter weeks. A handful of people worked longer hours regularly. In my experience these were mostly people who both really loved their job and had nothing else to do. After all, many Googlers started playing around with computers as a hobby at a young age. They never stopped, but now they get paid for it. For some people, though, this turned into a downward spiral towards burnout. Anyone who has done much computer programming knows there's a lot of frustration involved even when things are going relatively well. Success and completion always seem just a moment away, but a moment can stretch into hours. So for some folks, their passion makes them work so hard it's unsustainable. Eventually they either recognize what's happening and pull back, they develop mental health issues, or they snap quit one day. As a manager, part of my job is to not let things get to this point.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Last interview was informal with a manager I wouldn’t be reporting directly to. It was more like a conversation to get to know me. I passed all of the technical interviews. The last interview went very well. Does this imply that I will get the job?
Answer: In the tech industry, if you have completed a full round of technical interviews and are then asked to have an informal chat with a manager, it's both a good and bad sign. Usually this happens when the candidate did well in the interviews but for some reason can't be placed with the originally intended team. This happens sometimes when multiple great candidates interview for the same role, when there's a reorg, or when the original hiring manager thinks the person would be better in another role. So the good news is you did well in the interviews. Otherwise they wouldn't still be spending time on you. The bad news is that there's a significant chance they can't or don't want to hire you into the role you interviewed for. That said, it's also possible that they want to consider you for both roles, that the second manager is someone you'll work really closely with, or that there's an upcoming reorg in which you'll be moved to report to that manager.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How are the tech workers dealing with a decline in their equities?
Answer: In my experience, most people are grumbling and expect their employer to give large stock grants in this year's compensation cycle. If that doesn't happen there will be a lot of people who change jobs to a company that will pay them their true market value. There are certainly many people who have already done this. I think there's also been a tempering of expectations about how much upside to expect from stock grants. Although people would always have acknowledged that stocks don't always go up, they had certainly gotten used to it. This downturn has brought a little uncertainty back into their thinking.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is a Senior Software Engineer supposed to know?
Answer: A Senior Software Engineer is expected to know a subject area well enough that they can identify and solve problems in that area with no outside direction. They should know this area well enough that others ask questions of them about their area of expertise far more than they ask questions of others about it. This is not to say that they don't ask questions in general, only that they are expert within their defined area. They are expected to set the agenda for work to be done in their area. There isn't a precise definition of how big a subject area is required, and it varies by company. Generally, my experience is that the area should be complex enough that one person can't make adequate progress alone and must coordinate others to achieve their company's goals. Senior engineers are also expected to make others around them better, through mentoring, planning, coordination and other leadership. These are equally as important as technical skills for a Senior Engineer. And at higher levels these skills are typically even more important than technical skills.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Does the intelligence shared by the Five Eyes include information on citizens of their respective countries? Who has benefited the most among the five eyes?
Answer: This is one of the shady ways the Five Eyes' member agencies help each other: they can spy on each other's citizens. The NSA isn't legally allowed to spy on Americans. They use every bit of gray area in the law to their advantage, but they still don't just straight up spy on Americans. We know this from the Snowden leaks. But the Brits can spy on Americans, and the Brits can share what they learn with American intelligence agencies. So the Five Eyes consortium gives the NSA a way to legally spy on Americans. I'm not as familiar with the legal situation in the other Five Eyes countries but I imagine it's similar. America almost certainly benefits the most from this and other aspects of the Five Eyes, simply because it's the biggest and most geopolitically important.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Does Google hire open source contributors without college degrees?
Answer: Yes. But don't think of it as an easy alternative path. You can't substitute a few months of open source work for 4 years of college (unless you're truly brilliant). Open source on its own is unlikely to get you an interview unless it's the kind of very important thing lots of people have heard of, or if it's a project that's very important to Google. On the other hand, if you skipped college but have several years of solid work experience, you can certainly get an interview, and having some open source out there will help augment that resume.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the approximate value of all the perks that big tech companies provide to their employees? Do they have to declare that on their tax returns, and pay taxes on them?
Answer: Health insurance is generally worth about $10–15k annually. Free meals might be worth $10–50/day ($2500-12,500/year), depending on how many meals the employee eats at work and what exactly they eat. I used to eat like $10 in smoked salmon every day at breakfast at Google. It doesn't cost the company anything close to this much because they get insane bulk discounts. This perk isn't available anymore, since COVID. Snacks and soda are worth perhaps $5–10/day ($1250–2500/year). Massages at Google were worth a couple hundred dollars a year. You only got about one free one per year. The rest you had to pay for, although at a big discount. It's hard to value things like pool tables and video games, but it'd be hard to argue they're worth more than a couple hundred bucks a year. Employees do not pay tax on any of this, and for the most part neither does the company (in the US). The meals and snacks are considered to be for the benefit of the employer, because they encourage employees to stay at work for meals and thus work more. As such they aren't income to the employees and are deductible expenses for the company. I think things like pool tables are considered part of office decor. Some benefits are taxable. I think I had to pay a small amount of tax for the free massages. The company took care of all the accounting on that and I never had to think about it.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If Google gives an offer and we didn’t get a visa, will the offer be cancelled?
Answer: Yes, almost always. Offers are usually contingent on ability to obtain work clearance in the location of the job, so failure to obtain a visa means no job. Very rarely the person may be allowed to work from a different country. This won't be held against the candidate. Having received one Google offer, the candidate is likely to receive another if their visa situation changes.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the significance of Google acquiring Mandiant?
Answer: Google is getting very serious about competing in security. We should expect them to become a major player in this market. Mandiant is the top incident response consulting firm. They are the people you hire after a breach to show you're not pinching pennies. And they really are good, widely respected within the industry. In addition to incident response they provide a whole host of other cybersecurity services, such as evaluating your security against external standards and telling you what to fix. They have an army of consultants covering all things cybersecurity, and existing business deals with many large companies. Google also has Chronicle. Chronicle started out as an anomaly detection and data visualization tool, but has steadily grown in complexity. Google recently acquired SIEMplify, a startup SIEM company. [1]For those not familiar, a SIEM is a system for managing security alerts, identifying the most risky and giving responders tools to facilitate investigation and remediation. It also includes the ability to create automatic responses to alerts, running on Google Cloud of course. Google now has a nearly full set of tools to compete in the security market. They have big data tools in BigQuery and other Google Cloud systems that can run high scale detection alerting and forensic analysis. They have a SIEM. And they have a consulting team. They can match all of the high level capabilities of Splunk, the market leader, though Splunk still has more features, integrations and existing customers. Splunk is not the only competitor in this market. Crowdstrike, for example, is also building out a complete integrated security solution. So this market segment is getting hot, and it's clear Google intends to be a major player. This will be an interesting area to watch over the next few years.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do some companies like Google, Amazon, and Facebook have a no feedback policy when rejecting candidates?
Answer: In giving feedback to a rejected candidate, there is little to be gained and a lot to lose. A candidate who gets feedback and accepts it as valid may improve and someday become an employee. They may say nice things about your company to their friends, and they may be more likely to become your customer. But realistically, the odds that feedback actually turns into a meaningful benefit to the company are pretty small. On the other hand, there are tons of ways giving feedback can go wrong. The candidate may disagree with the feedback and say bad things about your company to their friends. They may become angry and abusive with the recruiter. Most significantly, they may perceive bias in the feedback and take legal action. Rejected job candidates tend to get upset, not surprisingly, and some of them in their anger pursue pretty dubious legal cases. This happens a lot less often if the company simply refuses to give feedback.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do you manage over 10+ people?
Answer: In a skilled labor role, 10 direct reports is about the most a single manager can handle, and that's pushing it. At around 8–10 reports, it starts to become very hard to observe each person's work enough to provide useful feedback and an accurate performance evaluation. A team of 10 likely has a bunch of different projects going on, so it's hard for the manager to keep close enough track of them to identify problems and correct them. It's hard to have team discussions and maintain good chemistry. And during performance reviews, managing 10+ people means 60+ hour weeks. At around 8–10 direct reports, it's time to hire another manager. This always presents a few problems. First, if you divide 10 reports among 2 managers, each has only 5 reports, a pretty small team. Small teams increase overhead, and managers with not enough to do often become micromanagers or start taking on there most interesting work themselves, leaving nothing for the team. Second, how do you divide up the teams? Often the dividing line winds up being pretty arbitrary. Third, does the new manager report to the old manager's manager or to the old manager, who becomes a manager of managers? The original manager's manager may not have room to take on a new report themselves, but the original manager may not be ready to become a manager of managers. These are all problems you have to sort out when a team grows to 10+ employees. One way to extend a manager's reach is through senior technical leaders. A senior tech lead can lead strategy discussions and be responsible for large projects involving many team members. That frees up the manager to focus on personnel matters, which lets them manage more people. But you can only really stretch them manager by 2–4 more people this way, and suitable senior leads are hard to find. Usually it's better just to hire another manager. In an unskilled labor role, it's possible to manage more people using metrics and rules. You tell them they need to make 80 widgets an hour and you fire them if they make 70. You're basically using them as human robots. I don't have a ton of experience with this kind of role so I won't comment further. In organizational design, the number of reports per manager is called the “span of control”. Upper management spends a lot of time trying to get the right span of control for their organization. Too many reports per manager means the managers don't do a great job. Too few reports per manager means too many managers, which wastes money and leads to employees becoming disconnected from the values and strategies upper management is trying to promote.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is your opinion of Google telling employees it won't raise employee pay to match inflation?
Answer: I think Google does actually intend to raise pay in line with inflation for most employees, but their non-committal phrasing was sensationalized by the media. According to CNBC, Google’s VP of compensation Frank Wagner told employees at a company all-hands meeting on December 7th that Google doesn’t “have any plans to do any type of across-the-board type adjustment” when asked about the inflation rate in the US. Wagner did hint that the company’s compensation budgets “reflected” the higher cost of labor that comes with increased prices, according to CNBC. However, he said that the company would rather pay any increased wages based on performance rather than do an increase across the board.[1] So what he actually said is: Most employees will get a raise that brings their salary roughly into line with their market value. Low performers will not. This lets low performers' pay decay to their market value in real terms. So there's really nothing interesting going on here. But that's not how it was reported, because boring doesn't sell.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What makes you most uncomfortable about sharing information about your wealth?
Answer: I’m quite wealthy by the standards of most Americans (>$1m) and not that wealthy by the standards of wealthy Americans (<$10m). There are a few reasons I don't tell people my income or wealth. I don't want them to feel like I'm trying to brag. I don't think having money makes me a better person, but some people assume that I would only talk about income or wealth to measure mine against theirs. I don't want to trigger some anxiety the other person might have about money or status. Some people assess their own worth based on how their income, wealth or consumption compares to others', how well they are “keeping up with the Joneses". While I don't think people should assess themselves this way, I still don't want to trigger those feelings. I don't want to be judged based on people's biases. Plenty of people think that all people with money are egotistical, greedy or even immoral, or that we hold some set of distasteful political beliefs. Like anyone else, I want to be thought of as an individual, not a member of a group. I worry about sending the wrong social cues. If we go out to lunch with someone much less wealthy than me, should I pick up the check? If I do, I might be implying that they can't afford to pay their share, which might make some people feel insulted or inadequate. If I don't, I might appear cheap. I usually pick it up because I figure a free lunch probably makes up for any minor insult. I worry that if word gets to the wrong person I could become a target for robbery. I wish I, and everyone, could talk more freely about income and wealth. I think transparency is helpful for society. I think keeping money matters secret implies that there is something that needs to be kept secret, and I think that reinforces some people's negative attitudes towards their own wealth. Maybe if we could talk freely about wealth, we might stop seeing it as a mark of status. A number of very real advantages come with wealth, some fair and many not, and I wish we could talk about them more openly. I'm honestly afraid about the comments I'm going to get on this answer. Please be nice.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the challenges managers face while doing a performance review in a hybrid work environment?
Answer: I actually think giving performance reviews remotely is better than it was in person. Performance review conversations can be quite anxiety producing for many employees. That's not ideal, because people have a harder time thinking rationally when their emotions are high. The artificiality of video conferences seems to reduce the intensity of the situation. I think people have an automatic physical response to being near another person that isn't triggered in the same way over video conference. Probably the biggest downside is that it's more difficult to read emotional responses. If the person is surprised or upset, it can be more difficult to tell. This is well known, but it's especially impactful in high stakes review conversations.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why does Google struggle to integrate experienced executives into their engineering teams?
Answer: Google has a very particular management culture. Individual engineers are given a ton of autonomy. Managers have much less control over technical and strategic decisions than at most other companies. Googlers have many job opportunities, so if they don't like what their manager is telling them to do, they can and will go get a job elsewhere. Furthermore, Google's technical infrastructure is unique and complex. Usually the technical expertise an executive has won't directly apply to Google's systems. Yet Google, and Googlers, expects managers to be quite technical. Executives hired from outside often fail to meet this expectation.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Can a student of a less reputed institute (to the Google standards) ever join Google?
Answer: Something like 10% of Google's engineers have no college degree at all. Plenty more went to lower rated colleges. In fact, the entire time I worked there, I think I knew maybe one other person who went to a top 20 school (I went to Dartmouth). I think the most prestigious school I ever saw on a resume was Johns Hopkins. No Ivy League, Stanford, MIT. What got these people into Google was one of two things. Some excelled academically at lower ranked schools. A 3.9 GPA in almost any university engineering program will get you an interview. But most Googlers I knew joined Google after demonstrating excellence in other jobs, or joined Google as a very low level employee and worked their way up. I knew multiple people who started as data center techs, swapping hard drives out, and were given progressively more skilled jobs as they demonstrated their ability. So no matter where you are now, if you want to join Google some day, you can do it.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do Google and Facebook have a plan to own the internet's infrastructure?
Answer: In one sense, not anymore. In another, they already do. Google Fiber, launched in 2012, was an attempt to build a high speed fiber network. It was intended to provide truly high speed internet at low prices, mainly to benefit Google's other businesses. To this day, many consumers are poorly served by a small number of monopoly ISPs. Google was trying to cut through that in order to get more people onto the internet and with higher bandwidth connections that could run the kind of data intensive services that Google excels at. Unfortunately, regulatory opposition was fierce. Comcast and its peers were very unhappy about Google's attempt to compete, and others were worried about the idea of Google controlling yet another aspect of the internet. Google found it very difficult to expand to new locations and ultimately ceased expanding the service in 2016, though it remains active after it had already launched. Google also had a plan, Project Loon, to provide internet from giant balloons, which would hover over an area and provide wifi — sort of halfway between a cell phone tower and satellite internet. Its main purpose was to provide internet to underserved areas that didn't have internet for technological and economic reasons, with the hope and expectation that these newly connected people would become Google customers. Google has a second program with the same mission, Google Station, which put wifi terminals in public places like train stations. However, cell phone technology and availability advanced quickly in developing markets, and both projects found themselves without enough of a market to survive. Station was cancelled in 2020 and Loon in 2021. Amazon has its own plan for satellite internet, Project Kuiper, which is just getting off the ground.[1] Their motivations are similar to Google's: to connect new users to the internet in the hope that they become customers. Because AWS powers much of the internet, this is almost certain. Relative to Google's efforts, Amazon has the advantage of entering the market at a time when satellite launches have become relatively cheap and routine. Facebook had a similar plan for satellite internet that they gave up on, and its the team of engineers joined Amazon in 2021. Facebook does still partner with other satellite internet providers on software. Unlike Amazon, which profits from nearly everything any internet user does, Facebook only profits from ads shown when those users use a Facebook platform. That makes this type of speculative venture less profitable. In an odd way, the tech giants (mostly Amazon) do provide much of the internet's infrastructure through their Content Delivery Networks (CDNs). CDNs are servers located throughout the globe in order to be closer to the end users and thereby reduce latency and bandwidth cost. Static parts of the site, like images, are cached, while dynamic content is rendered centrally in a data center and sent to them CDN server to deliver to the user. A number of CDNs are available, including from AWS, Azure, GCP and Akamai. When you visit a site hosted by the AWS CDN, Amazon owns all of the infrastructure except the connection from your computer to the CDN server (with some exceptions). So in a weird way, Amazon, Microsoft and Google already own much of the infrastructure of the internet.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How does claiming an ethnicity work on applications? Couldn't anyone claim any ethnicity?
Answer: In the US, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) requires that employers ask a specific set of questions about gender, race, ethnicity and a few other things, and report the results to the government. They do this in order to track statistics and identify companies that are way out of line with statistical expectations, like a company that hires 1000 men and zero women. The options are fixed: every company asks the same questions. The answers are self-identified: nobody will double check. In fact, it is illegal to use this information to influence a hiring decision, with only rare and narrow exceptions. You can indeed claim any ethnicity, but it won't matter. There is an option to answer “Prefer not to answer". When a candidate chooses this, the company is required to guess! This is required because there may be patterns to who chooses not to answer, and those patterns could indicate biased hiring. Kind of crazy if you ask me. The standard questions have some problems. “Latino" is not included among the choices of race. Instead, there's a separate yes/no “Are you Hispanic?” question. The race choices are also missing the Middle East entirely: there is no option for Jewish, Arab or Persian. The Asian option lumps together everyone from Indians to Maori. There is no biracial option. There is an Other box, which is what I usually check and put “Jewish", although I'm only half Jewish. Some employers, including many tech companies, have started asking a much wider range of questions with more options, including LGBTQ status and more detailed questions about race and ethnicity. These are always optional and have no bearing on hiring decisions. No one involved in hiring can see the answers. They do this to gather data about their potential and actual workforce and to identify bias in their recruiting and hiring patterns. To repeat: these questions have no bearing on who gets hired, even indirectly. The statistics that come from these surveys are very tightly controlled within the company. I'm not a lawyer and this is a very complex area of law, so please don't make important decisions because of something you read on Quora.

Name: David Seidman
Question: A CEO fires 900 employees over Zoom, just before the holidays. What do you think?
Answer: Before I looked up the situation the question refers to[1], I already knew the answer: this company is screwed. There's only two ways something like this happens: the company's financial situation is extremely dire and/or the CEO is a total asshole. Sometimes this kind of mass layoff at holiday time happens when the company is doing terribly and simply runs out of money. They've held onto the people as long as they could, but there is just no more money in the bank to pay them with. Companies in that situation rarely recover. This is usually the beginning of the end — and very often, though not always, the people involved all saw it coming. The second possibility is that the CEO is a huge jerk, someone who doesn't care about ruining the holidays for 900 people just to save a couple paychecks. Most CEOs are nicer than that and plan major org changes to avoid the holiday season. Even for underperformaning individuals, I've always ensured that no PIP would end over the holidays or be delivered right before them. It's not just compassion to do that, although compassion certainly plays a big role. It's also good business. Right now the remaining employees have two thoughts running through their heads. 1: Our boss is an asshole. 2: Who's next? Anyone who can find a new job is going to do so ASAP before they get caught up in the next round of playoffs. Nobody who remains is going to put out their best effort. Laying off 10% of employees now rather than in January saves roughly 1% of annual payroll. Do you think this is going to cost more than 1% productivity from the remaining employees? You better believe it. Dumb, dumb, dumb. Which brings me back to: this company is screwed.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What makes a bad IT security engineer?
Answer: Lack of an attacker mindset. Everyone in security needs to be able to think like a bad guy, to operate with the attitude that rules were made to be broken. If you can't see all the ways an attacker might move through your network, you can't stop them or catch them. It is an absolute requirement. And it can't be taught, as far as I can tell. I've seen several attempts. A person who lacks the right mindset may be able to stay in the industry but will never be a strong performer. There is one exception: compliance. Compliance is about following rules, not breaking them. It's very different from other branches of security and requires a different skill set.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Facebook changing its name to metaverse? Why metaverse?
Answer: They haven't officially given a reason, but here's my take: Mark Zuckerberg sees a future where the metaverse of science fiction is real, and he thinks Facebook should be the ones to create it. He's right. Facebook controls multiple top social network and a top VR gaming company. No other company has a portfolio like that. And those are probably the key elements required for a real metaverse: the physical apparatus, game software to create the universe, and a network of social connections so that users have something to do. If digital relationships start to become as important as real life relationships, Facebook use uniquely positioned to provide that service. This seems intentional, in that the purchase of Oculus didn't have a clear relationship to Facebook's business at the time, but it makes perfect sense in light of this metaverse strategy. Microsoft could conceivably compete. They have XBox, Hololense and XBox Live, which is a sort of social network. One possible path to the metaverse is through gaming. After all, World of Warcraft and other MMORPGs are basically metaverses. Maybe one of them will evolve into non-gaming use. Still, Hololense isn't part of Xbox and Xbox Live isn't a full fledged social network, so Facebook is still better positioned. Conversely, a metaverse not controlled by Facebook could be hugely damaging to Facebook's business. If digital relationships start to become as important as real life relationships, and Facebook is not where those digital relationships take place, the value of Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and WhatsApp all decreases hugely. Whoever controls the metaverse will know much more about social connections than Facebook, and Facebook's importance and utility will be substantially diminished. The other possible explanation is that Mark Zuckerberg just really thinks a multiverse would be cool. 50% chance that that's the real reason.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Facebook's rebranding to Meta similar to Google's reorganization as Alphabet?
Answer: No, they are fundamentally different. Google's reorganization into Alphabet was primarily a financial maneuver. By splitting out speculative businesses like Waymo and Loon from core Google search, the Alphabet structure provided better accounting for investors and more freedom for Alphabet sub-brands to come and go without risking the Google brand. By contrast, Facebook's change to Meta is purely a rebranding. It has no direct impact on financial matters and doesn't change the relationship between business units within Meta. Meta did say they're going to split out VR revenue, which increases transparency for investors and is a signal that they view VR as a significant revenue generator in the future. One similarity with Alphabet/Google is that the name of the company will now be different from the name of its main product. This makes it easier to maintain multiple separate brand identities.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How much opportunity does someone have to transfer internally from an SRE to a security engineer position in Google, especially if he got rejected from this security role before (external application)?
Answer: When I worked for Google security, I worked with several former SREs who had converted to security. I also ran a rotation program where SWEs, SREs and other technical folks spent 6 months with the security team as a trial and learning experience. Some of them stayed and converted to security engineers. If you were rejected as a security engineer but hired as an SRE, you've been accepted as meeting Google's technical bar in general, but your security knowledge wasn't up to snuff (or at least that's what the interviewers thought). You'll need to learn whatever it was that you were missing and convince a manager in the security org to hire you. Or perhaps the rotation program is still happening, in which case that would be a good path. Overall, a person who was able to get hired by Google will probably be able to transition to Security Engineer without too much trouble, but it may take some work.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the strangest reaction of someone who has just been fired?
Answer: I had two friends get laid off from Microsoft when their business unit shut down. One of them shook the HR person's hand and enthusiastically said, “Thank you so much!!!” The second came out of the meeting with a huge smile and told me, “I just got laid off. It's my lucky day!” They had both been planning to quit already — one to relocate, the other to go to business school — and now they would get paid severance to do it. The second had even told his manager but hadn't given official notice yet.

Name: David Seidman
Question: When hackers try to break a password by means of 'brute force', what length do they limit themselves?
Answer: It's rare today for anyone to simply guess random passwords. Instead, they use dictionaries of the most common passwords, created from publicly and privately known database breaches. They are usually sorted by probability. Sometimes they are filtered by the target site’s password complexity requirements and sometimes not. How big a dictionary to use is one of the key decisions a brute force attacker must make. Using a larger dictionary means a lower average chance of cracking an account per attempt, because more time is spent on low probability guesses, but a higher maximum number of compromised accounts once all guesses are tried. In some contexts, like cryptocurrency, better protected accounts also tend to be worth more on average. Two of the big limitations on brute forcing are practical: it is hard to obtain good dictionaries and to implement an effective piece of brute force malware. Widely available password dictionaries have usually already been used against any conceivable target site, so there's nothing new left to compromise. But getting a private dictionary requires knowing the right people and paying them. Even once you have a good dictionary, you need botnet software sophisticated enough to deliver the attack without being blocked and with maximum efficiency. Creating that kind of software takes effort and skill. Some bad guys don't have those things and are limited to dumber attacks. There are rare times when an attacker has compromised a database of hashed password and can guess very rapidly without worrying about detection. In these cases, after they've run through their password dictionary, they'll try truly random passwords for the accounts that haven't been cracked yet. They start with just a few characters (e.g. 6), or whatever the required minimum was, if they know that. Because the number of possible passwords grows exponentially as the number of characters increases, in most circumstances attackers won't try more than 10 or 12 characters, but this is completely determined by the attacker's goals and resources.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What qualifications will give me a better shot at landing an internship in cyber security?
Answer: Good grades are critical. It's one of the only verifiable and measurable things in your resume. If you have the opportunity to do a thesis on cyber security, do so. You may get a job directly related to your thesis, and even if not, you'll have valuable knowledge that will help you in interviews and on the job. Hiring managers know that and value it A good recommendation from a professor is huge. Professors don't give them out without reason. The reference is much more valuable if you have worked with that professor on something, ideally closely, for a long time and on an ongoing basis. Open source contributions are very valuable as well, especially to the organizations that sponsor the project you're contributing to. Even small contributions show that you're able to work on a shared codebase and took the effort to do so. Larger contributions are even more compelling. Work experience of any kind is helpful in getting any internship because it shows you know how to be an employee: showing up to work every day, interacting with peers and managers, being responsible for job duties, etc. Specific to cyber security, if you have any CVE credits or bug bounties as an undergraduate, you will jump to the head of the line for appsec jobs. If you have published novel threat intelligence research or reverse engineered malware or exploits, you will similarly be a hot commodity for relevant jobs. If you have excess money and time, you can take certification courses. They will show that you are interested enough to put in the effort and that you have some basic knowledge. That said, certifications are a terribly inefficient way to break into the industry as an undergraduate.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why did David Seidman leave Google?
Answer: I got a big promotion, basically. My job at Salesforce is what my boss’s job was at Google. Instead of running part of the detection team, I get to run all of it. The promotion came with a big compensation increase too. It was an opportunity I couldn’t refuse. And it was unlikely I’d get a similar opportunity at Google simply because I had reached the level of management where I needed someone above me in the org chart to leave in order to open up a spot, and it didn’t seem likely any of them were going to. There was nothing at all wrong with my job at Google. I really loved it there and could see myself returning someday, if the circumstances were right. At this stage of my career, there are only a few jobs at the right level of management in the right subject area, so it’s pretty unlikely that one of them will come open at the same time that I am looking for a change myself. But you never know.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is a dirty secret about layoffs?
Answer: Layoffs are usually described by the company either as a way to reduce costs or to exit an unsuccessful line of business. But in truth, they are often used to clean out a bunch of low performers all at once. Some companies have a policy that the bottom 10% of performers get fired every year. This ensures a high performance standard but also disincentivizes taking risks and sometimes fires good employees who had a bad year. So many companies intentionally avoid that kind of forced culling. But the opposite effect then takes hold: with nothing forcing managers to fire marginal low performers, they tend to accumulate. Good performers tend to have lots of job opportunities, so they leave, while bad performers are stuck. The worst get fired, but on average managers tend to be reluctant to fire people, even when it's deserved, so you wind up with an excess number of people who do just enough to not get fired. But if the company has a layoff and every manager has to fire the bottom 10% as a one time thing, the company gets rid of those lower performers without the kind of long term cultural damage that an annual culling policy creates. There are certainly short term repercussions and costs, including loss of good employees on strong teams with no low performers, and it has to be a one-time thing to work, but within those bounds it does work. You'll often see this kind of layoff when a new CEO takes over a struggling company. A second major benefit of using layoffs to fire low performers is that there's much less risk of a lawsuit. It's harder for someone to allege that they were illegally targeted for firing when many people are laid off simultaneously. But companies will never tell you this.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why would tech companies prefer to hire an H-1B employee from India as compared to a qualified professional within the USA or a US citizen?
Answer: The big tech companies companies don't. Let me tell you all the hassles that come with hiring and employing an H1B employee. When you're hiring, if you decide to hire a candidate who needs an H1-B candidate is your best option, you are gambling that the candidate is actually going to get the visa. You're going to have to wait several months for the approval process. You're going to spend on the order of $10k in legal costs and fees, not counting the massive amounts of your own time you'll need to spend on paperwork. You get neither the time nor the money back if the candidate doesn't get the visa, which is the most likely outcome. Once you have successfully gotten a candidate hired on an H1-B visa, you've got a few years of smooth sailing — as long as the candidate doesn't move, change job titles or duties, get too big a raise, or any of several other changes that can trigger a reevaluation of the visa. If your employee wants to return home for any reason, they may not be able to return. I knew one guy who got stuck in his home country for a year! And he was British — not exactly a refugee. As you approach the end of your three years of relatively smooth sailing, go back to step 1: you have to apply again for a visa renewal. The government will not tell you how long this will take. If it gets denied your employee will have a very short amount of time to leave the country. It's not like we save on salary costs by hiring from overseas. We pay employees on visas using the same salary bands as for US citizens. We couldn't legally do otherwise, but also, you don't get the best work out of people by underpaying them. Many managers won't even consider candidates who need visas. I don't know anyone who would prefer to hire a candidate who needs a visa over one who doesn't. That would be absolutely crazy. We hire candidates on visas, which we only do rarely, because we can't find an equally qualified and skilled American. I get a lot of rude comments on answers about visas, so please keep it civil or expect to be blocked. Polite disagreement is welcome.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Who earns more—a software engineer or attorney?
Answer: I have enough good friends who are attorneys to estimate the earnings of my peers, and I know engineer salaries very well. My experience is with higher end law firms and tech companies in big cities, so that's what I'm talking about here. Attorneys make very different amounts of money depending on where they live and what kind of law they practice. At the low end, a government attorney handling procedural matters might make under six figures — less than a college hire at a FANG company. On the upper end, a partner corporate law attorney in NYC with lots of experience can make several million (tens of millions+ at the highest end). The average attorney is obviously somewhere in between. A midcareer attorney at a very good firm makes a few hundred thousand a year (“a few hundred thousand " is kind of a crazy thing to say — that's a huge amount of money). A senior partner will make $1m+, but I'm not sure beyond that. Software engineers start out making less than entry level attorneys. But since an attorney has to be in school 3 years longer than an engineer, by the time a lawyer enters the workforce an engineer from the same undergraduate graduation year has 3 years of experience. By that point they will likely be making about as much as the entry level attorney, assuming average performance. As they advance in their careers, attorneys start to make increasingly more than engineers, on average and even for high performers. Engineers work fewer hours, though, so their hourly rates are roughly comparable. The high end gets weird. Partners typically make more than a very senior engineer or manager, but tech executives and the very best engineers can make more than law partners. Law partners are required to spend a lot of time finding new business, which many find distasteful. But partners usually have the option to work fewer hours late in their career, while engineers at the peak of their careers work more hours in my experience. Lawyers pretty much top out in the tens of millions, but engineers who found startups can make hundreds of millions or rarely even billions. So it's hard to say who makes “more” on average at this career stage.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Which Facebook employee likely had the longest day after the site went down?
Answer: It's hard to overstate how big a deal this outage is. The entire time the site is down, the company is not making money. They lost about $50m this way. More importantly, it destroyed trust in the platform. Plenty of people who are choosing between WhatsApp and Signal or Oculus and Sony, for example, are now going to pick Facebook's competitor. Facebook also has a nascent Workplace service which I would say is now dead in the water. No business can afford a 6 hour outage — that's just absolutely unacceptable. Almost certainly everyone on the teams directly responsible for creating and fixing the incident worked continuously from the moment it was discovered until they dropped from exhaustion. This includes everyone in all the related management chains up through Zuckerberg. Even once the incident was resolved, there will be an immediate focus on making sure the site doesn't go back down for any reason and on identifying and remediating the multiple problems that combined to cause the outage. They will probably have a production change moratorium in place, which requires a ton of work across the company to change every plan to roll out new features this week. That will impact marketing and sales as well as engineering, though only to the extent that new launches were planned for this week. The role of incident commander, responsible for coordinating everyone working on the incident, will have changed hands a few times. Incident response teams are prepared for this sort of thing and have procedures to hand off to a fresh person periodically. Exhausted incident commanders don't do their best work. So those folks will not have been as badly worked into the ground. The customer support and sales teams were probably working non-stop too. They probably did log off voluntarily after an extended business day because customers tend to go to sleep at night themselves (for any given time zone). The single person who had it worst is probably the head of reliability. I'm not sure exactly how their org is structured, but there's certainly a single person, a senior executive, who has full and total accountability for the site staying up. That person not only has to deal with every part of the outage, they also have to worry about losing their job.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How would you rank the CEOs of Microsoft?
Answer: It's pretty clear: Bill Gates started the whole thing. He went from a kid in a dorm room to the richest person on earth. He was CEO when Microsoft introduced DOS, Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Exchange, Internet Explorer, Visual Studio, Xbox and MSPaint. He went out on top. Steve Ballmer presided over the decline of most of Microsoft's products. By the time he left, Windows was so out of favor that they literally couldn't give it away, IE was displaced by Chrome, and Xbox One was on track to lose to PlayStation. Only the business-oriented products remained strong. Along the way, he blew billions chasing search (Bing), audio (Zune), tablets (Surface), and mobile (Nokia). And he created a toxic work culture that drove away many talented employees. He did set in motion two key products for Microsoft's future: Azure and Surface. He should get credit for that. But it was Satya Nadella who turned those products, along with a revitalized Office, into massive growth. Microsoft is once again one of the most valuable companies on the planet. It successfully transitioned from being a company that sells software in boxes to a subscription-based cloud provider. Surface has become a first class line of business. Nadella's big acquisitions, LinkedIn and GitHub, have maintained their value and added a sensible amount of integration with Microsoft's ecosystem. There have been no multi-billion dollar debacles. I don't see how anyone could arrive at a different ordering than Gates > Nadella > Ballmer. Though I'm sure plenty of commenters will try. :)

Name: David Seidman
Question: What should I major in if I want to work in the tech industry such as Facebook and Google?
Answer: Computer Science, no question. Google hires all kinds of people for all kinds of work, but it has more trouble hiring engineers than any other role. If you have any talent for software development, or related fields like data science or security, that's the best way in. If computers aren't your thing, you might consider marketing or sales, since tech companies of all sizes hire lots of those people as well. There's more competition for these positions, but they are probably second best to engineering.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How fast do Google employees get a replacement or new laptop/phone if it’s broken? Is there a KPI on these requests?
Answer: There are loaner laptops readily available, so if your laptop breaks you use one of those while they get you a new laptop, which can take a couple days. They were cheap Chromebooks, but serviceable in a pinch. Everyone I knew who had a company-paid phone used their personal device and just had the company pay the bills. Beta versions of upcoming Pixel phones were much coveted, but the downside was that if it broke you might not get another one, ever, or not for a long time, because they didn't manufacture many of them.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why are Facebook and Google still trusted after all the spying scandals?
Answer: Because most people know the quid pro quo they're signing up for: you give up your data, you get free web search and social media. And email, and maps, and… Most people aren't particularly sensitive about their privacy on most topics, though things like personal finances and medicine are a different story. So they don't really mind that Google knows they like vintage Russian dolls or triathlons. “Who cares?” is the typical attitude. Politics is one of the exceptions. When Facebook screwed that up with Cambridge Analytica, they did pay a price. After the scandal, trust in Facebook dropped by a whopping 66%.[1] The stock dropped 20% and user growth was at its lowest rate ever, [2] with growth mostly coming overseas where the scandal is less relevant. A small portion of the population, perhaps 1%, cares very strongly about privacy in all things, and most of the population cases strongly about privacy in some things. But on average, people just don't care.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What do mediocre employees do that the best employees don't do?
Answer: “Not my job" Mediocre employees show up every day, do a fine job, collect their paycheck and go home. When work arises that's outside of their job description, they shrug and say “sorry, can't help you with that.” There is nothing wrong with this — the company is getting what it's paying for. Great employees take ownership. They say, “let me figure this out" or “let me find the person who can help" — and they do. If they transfer a problem to someone else to resolve, great employees check in to make sure that person is doing a good job. Great employees don't just do work, they solve problems, whether it's their job or not. It's true that some companies don't pay any more for great work than they do for mediocre work. Those companies tend to find themselves without great workers. Edit: I’ve gotten many comments to the effect of, “But employers don’t reward good workers, so why put in the extra effort?” Read the last sentence again: when great workers aren’t rewarded, they go to work somewhere else. There are almost always plenty of job opportunities for high performers. Caveat: I can only speak for the North American and Western European job markets; things may be different elsewhere.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some secrets about working for big tech companies that you didn't know before joining those companies?
Answer: All those complaints you have about their products? The people working there complain about the same exact things. Microsoft employees complain about how slow Outlook is. Google employees complain about everything changing all the time. Salesforce employees complain about how hard our products are to use. So why don't we do something about it? There are a few possible answers: But none of that keeps the employees from complaining.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What should be the first step I should take if I am informed that my personal data with a company has been leaked?
Answer: Sign up for the free credit monitoring. Most likely your info will never be used, either because not enough sensitive data was stolen or because, with millions of victims, the attackers won't get around to stealing from all of them You may also want to stop doing business with the company. No company's cyber security is perfect, but some companies are better than others.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do tech companies care about personal projects when hiring programmers and engineers?
Answer: Yes, absolutely. Personal coding projects on a resume make it stand out. I almost always browse the repo of any decent candidate who has one. If there's significant code there, it's a big plus. However, it can work against you if your code sucks. If I look at your latest code and it has obvious bugs, I'm a lot less likely to give you an interview. If all of your commit messages are “fix bug”, “really fix bug this time", and “asdf", you're not showing good engineering practice, and I'm less likely to hire you for any position beyond entry level.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do so many people want to remain working remotely and not return to the office?
Answer: Most of my team members who want to stay remote cite the following reasons: They generally don't mind the physical environment at home and are fine with the loss of water cooler socializing. Not everyone wants to remain remote but these are the common reasons for people who do.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do internal recruiters often low ball candidates for a software engineering position?
Answer: The recruiter wants to make the lowest offer that the candidate will accept. Very few candidates will outright reject a lowball offer, unless they have other offers. In a noncompetitive situation, most candidates who think their offer is too low will negotiate and demand more. The company can then decide whether to pay it, stick with their initial offer, or something in between. In my experience companies are only willing to do one round of negotiation unless the candidate is extraordinary. After that it becomes “take it or leave it”. Usually the second offer is the best one the company is willing to make. There may sometimes be more negotiation about nonmonetary things like working from home (pre-COVID), which may even take place after the offer is accepted. In a competitive situation, the company will usually make its best offer immediately. Or, sometimes, the company will make a middling offer while asking the candidate for proof of the competing offer. This catches candidates who are exaggerating the competitive offer, which happens occasionally and would happen more if companies didn't guard against it. A company that lowballs a candidate in a competitive situation will likely lose the candidate, which means throwing away all the time spent recruiting them and leaving the position unfilled for longer. Larger companies will generally have an allowable offer and salary range for a given position. For entry level employees this may be completely fixed, with no negotiation allowed. The recruiter also needs to satisfy the hiring manager. The hiring manager has considerations other than saving money. If the candidate's salary is lower than their market rate, the manager will need to raise it before the candidate (now employee) figures that out, becomes unhappy and probably leaves. Raises often come from a smaller pool of money than initial offers, so managers would rather make a decent initial offer that will keep the employee happy. I've generally had the opposite problem: we make a big offer to a candidate, then that person is surprised when they don't get further raises. This may be biased because my experience is at big tech companies with highly competitive candidates, though.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What was the most ungrateful reaction you've seen when an employee got a raise?
Answer: In all my years of management, I've never had anyone express any negative sentiment after hearing their raise and bonus. Even low performers who didn't get much raise or bonus didn't expect to, and were often happy to get anything at all. There is one exception. I had an employee who was promoted from hourly to salaried. I was really happy for him, until he told me that his take home pay actually went down! He had been working a lot of overtime, which was unusual, and when he went on salary he stopped being eligible for overtime pay. So even though his base compensation went up, his actual compensation went down. We found a way to make it right with him.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What did tech giants discover after more than a year of mostly remote work?
Answer: There are some widely agreed discoveries and some widely agreed open questions. Remote work isn't a total disaster. It's at most a minor downgrade, most of the time, and in many ways and for many people it's an upgrade. There is much less commuting overhead, it's easier to work your hobbies into your workday, it's easier to travel (within what COVID allows), and you see your family more. We are learning over time to be more effective. We're getting better at using all the features of Zoom/Meet/Teams. We're figuring out ways to gather socially and to encourage innovation and spontaneity. Those improvements are accelerating as the software improves and becomes more widely available and as good ideas spread throughout the industry. New employees and junior employees are often struggling quite a bit. They aren't picking up on cultural norms or building connections. Because this often affects only one team member at a time, it can fly under the radar. The shift to remote work and generally remote everything is completely disrupting almost every company's business model. A quality online experience is suddenly a critical part of many traditional businesses' customer demand, and businesses are adding pickup and delivery features across the board, all of which depends on new technology. Customer bases are shifting radically too, as businesses like bars go bankrupt while companies making webcams are getting rich overnight. It's clear many of these changes will be permanent. The divide between knowledge workers and service workers is even more apparent and troubling than before. “I'm fortunate to be able to work remotely" is almost a cliche now. But it hasn't stopped us from ordering from DoorDash and Amazon constantly. The long term effects of remote work are still unknown. Whether a company commits to permanent remote work or a hybrid model, either way is a gamble. The main exception is companies whose business model is tied to remote work. There is zero chance Zoom is going to require their employees to come to an office. Similarly uncertain is the pay model. Right now companies are still paying more to people who live in high cost of living areas. Employees are upset about that, because their labor is equally valuable to the company regardless of where they live. It's unclear how this will be resolved.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What can you do about a senior engineer who is suddenly unwilling to do extra work they used to do after being denied promotion?
Answer: The answer is pretty simple. There is a performance expectation that they need to meet to remain employed — period. Three conversation might go something like: “As a senior engineer, you are expected to do X and Y. Since your promotion was denied, you have stopped doing X. I understand that you're disappointed, but reacting in this way will not help you achieve your career goals and may even result in formal performance management and termination. How can I help you get back on track?” If the person was previously performing above expectations and now is only meeting them, but not falling below what's required, the conversation can be altered to say: “Previously you were rated as a high performer, and your bonus reflected that. Your performance since your promotion was denied has fallen. It still meets the minimum requirement for your level, but if you continue performing as is you'll no longer be rated highly and can expect your bonus and future raises to reflect that decrease.” It's very helpful for these conversations to have a clearly written standard of performance and to have regular check-ins with team members in which you tell the employee how they're performing relative to the standard. Edit: A few commenters have pointed out that this is not an empathetic response. Great point! That’s an artifact of writing it down. In real life, you’d want to address the person’s individual attitude and history. Are they generally temperamental and this is an instance of a pattern? Was this a deserved promotion or a stretch, and did they know that? How does this promotion fit into their career history? What is their motivation for wanting it: prestige, money, authority, recognition, sense of advancement? And it’s always appropriate to say, “I understand how disappointing this is for you and how hard it is to stay motivated after getting denied a promotion. I’ve been there. We all want you to succeed and get promoted at the next opportunity. Here’s how we do that…” However, it’s really important to convey the performance message as well. The person needs to be totally clear on how their performance compares to the standard, because the decrease in performance will result in tangible consequences, and that should never be a surprise. I’m also assuming that the “hard work” referenced in the question equates to “higher performance”. If the person was previously working harder and not getting any better results, then working less to get the same result is a good thing.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do tech giants like Google and Facebook have such high turnover rates (<2 years) when the pay is high and benefits (free food, etc.) are good?
Answer: They don't have anything like that high a turnover rate. The study that claimed such high turnover was based on job change updates on LinkedIn. But when someone doesn't quit, there is no update. So the study only encompasses those who change jobs. What this statistic actually tells us is that people tend to either leave quickly or stick around for a long time. When people do leave, they often go to another FAANG or similar company. Or they go to startups in search of a bigger scope of impact and a big payday. When I worked at Google or Microsoft, I never knew anyone who left on good terms to take a job that was worse than the one they had.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If there wasn't ever Google, would Yahoo be as big as Google became?
Answer: No. Yahoo had completely the wrong model of how people would interact with the internet. Yahoo was based on a directory model, where computer-assisted humans would curate the most popular websites. If a user wanted to find sites about death metal, they would navigate to Music->Metal->Death. Searches would be run against this database. Google's model was driven by algorithms and focused on search. Because there was no human in the loop, Google could index a much larger set of pages, which turned out to be very important as the number of pages grew very rapidly. And it also turned out that people prefer to search for things rather than browse for them. So Yahoo couldn't have become Google without abandoning its core business model, which would never have happened. In fact, when Yahoo began to realize they had picked the wrong model, they ultimately had to license their search capability from AltaVista. That's the company that probably would have become the dominant search engine if Google didn't exist

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why does Google use so many "perma-temps" instead of hiring actual employees?
Answer: There are a few reasons Google teams hire contractors: The last two are the kind that typically become “permatemps". The scenario I've seen most often is that a team hires a contractor because they have spare cash budget but not headcount. It's easier to get cash for a contractor than headcount because budget is a one time expense while headcount is a long term commitment. You're only supposed to use cash for truly temporary positions, and that's usually how it starts out. But this year's temporary need often turns into next year's temporary need, the budget is renewed and the individual contractor stays employed. This can go on for several years quite easily. The second scenario I've seen is a happy one: the contractor is in a position with no career path and they're perfectly happy with that. Nobody is pushing them to get promoted or work overtime. They get a decent paycheck without worrying about the rat race. A variation on this is the person who likes the inconsistency of contract work. I once knew a guy who worked for Microsoft on a new 9 month contract every year so he could have the whole summer off. The third scenario I've seen is a much less happy one: a person who desperately wants to work for Google but can't pass the interviews takes a series of temporary contracts in the hope of impressing someone and getting hired. That can be a good way into Google, to be sure, but if it hasn't happened after the first few contracts, it's probably not going to. But people continue to chase the dream.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Should American companies continue to do business as usual with China if the Chinese government repeatedly hacks into the US government and businesses’ computer systems?
Answer: “Business as usual" already reflects companies' distrust of China. Many companies have separate “China only" laptops and phones. If you travel to China, you are temporarily issued a new laptop with nothing on it. Your account may even be locked while you're traveling. If not, you'll likely be blocked from connecting to the VPN from Chinese IP addresses. Every IT security team is concerned about being targeted by Chinese government hacking groups. They are a highly skilled adversary with a very broad mission. They're not the only such adversary but they're in the very top tier. But everyone knows it's not personal (most of the time). They're a spy agency doing what spy agencies do. So you defend against it as best you can. It's not connected to your company doing business in China (muost of the time), but rather your geopolitical importance on the global scale. So stopping doing business with China just hurts your profits for no gain. One exception is when companies use their geopolitical importance to pressure China to reduce its hacking. The most notable example is Google's withdrawal from China in 2010 following a Chinese attack. Most likely Google hoped China would agree to reduce their hacking activity in a way that would allow Google to return, although it turns out that didn't happen. So sometimes companies do actually stop doing business with China as a result of hacking. But it's very rare.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Silicon Valley has "Extremely leftist politics. For some that's an attraction but on average it's a negative". David Seidman said this in one of his answers. What does this exactly mean?
