Answer: If you plot American political positions on a one dimensional scale between “left” and “right", the average political belief of a San Francisco resident is very far to the left. Being far to the left, the average American is more conservative than the average San Francisco resident. The difference is pretty large. Most people prefer to live in a place where the residents have similar political beliefs. It's nice to feel normal. For the average person, San Francisco is not that.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How different is what you do for a living from what your parents did for a living?
Answer: When they were just out of school, my parents were elementary school teachers. I would be awful at that. My dad got his PhD and became a manager at tech companies. Pretty much exactly what I am. Later in life he became an entrepreneur, starting a business consulting firm that he's run for something like 20 years now. I like the idea of entrepreneurship but not the financial instability or the very hard work required. For a while in the 80s my dad worked for Silicon Graphics. When their business declined, they sold their office park, and it eventually wound up opened by Google. Both my brother's team and the California branch of my team were located there. So my brother and I wound up spending a lot of time in the same buildings my dad had worked in 25 years before. My mom was a full time parent for most of my childhood. She had a side hustle selling baskets in what was basically a multilevel marketing scheme. She was assistant manager at a clothing store for a while. Then she became really active as a volunteer docent at the art museum and that became her full time activity. I could not imagine something I'm less qualified for.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If big tech companies continue to allow for remote work in the future, is it in their best interest to pay engineers more/less based on where they choose to reside?
Answer: My prediction is that engineers will wind up getting paid equally wherever they live, and it will be less than tech hub salaries today. Let's look at the basic economics here. A company will only pay the minimum it has to, which is determined by its labor market. In the past, the labor market was defined by physical location. A San Francisco company had to hire engineers living in San Francisco or willing to move there. Because San Francisco is an expensive place to live, engineers demand higher salaries to live there. A Seattle company can offer a smaller salary that still leaves the employee with more money in their pocket after rent and taxes. But to get it, that person has to move to Seattle. Most people aren't willing to relocate, especially not repeatedly. So companies mostly hired from the city they were located in and people mostly worked for companies located in their city. But now, the labor market is national. A San Francisco company can pay a Seattle engineer Seattle prices — or that engineer can move 2 hours outside the city and live in a mansion on a lake with an even smaller salary. That person is now going to be willing to accept less pay than when they lived in a big city, just as today Seattle engineers make a bit less than San Francisco engineers and Indianapolis engineers make a lot less. This means that salaries will fall below tech hub levels, since companies can hire more cheaply elsewhere. Individuals now have more companies to choose from too. Companies that offer too little salary for a given type of position will not be able to hire effectively compared to their competitors. And that competition will happen across the nation, if not the world. So, all else equal, employers will have to offer the same salary everywhere to keep up with the competition. Bringing those two things together means tech companies will have to pay the same salary everywhere and it will be lower than tech hub salaries today.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do you think Mark Zuckerberg will ever step down from Facebook willingly?
Answer: Yes. Every other person who founded a giant, massively profitable product company has eventually retired. Bill Gates, Larry and Sergey of Google, and now Jeff Bezos have all stepped back from their companies. Their statements have been remarkably similar: they all see other problems they want to go solve, usually philanthropic or futuristic. I think Zuckerberg is going to do the same thing. This is assuming he doesn't die prematurely like Steve Jobs, of course.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Other than an H1-B visa, is there any option that an American company can hire someone from India?
Answer: I'm not a lawyer but I do deal with visa issues somewhat frequently. This answer is based on my experience. H1-B is the most common class of visa, but there are several others that get used. Probably the most common is the L-1. To qualify, you must work for the company outside the US in a specialized position for one year, then transfer into the US. The criteria are otherwise similar to an H1-B, but there's no cap, so most people who qualify do get one. Microsoft used to have a building in Vancouver, Canada where immigrants would work for a year in order to qualify for the L-1. Another type I've seen is the O-1 visa for “aliens of extraordinary ability". It's intended for people like Nobel Prize winners, but very talented engineers can qualify. Generally these are people with a significant public profile, like conference keynotes and published papers. Students in the US on a F-1 student visa often qualify for an OPT extension to the visa, which lets them work for one year, or three if in a STEM field. Then they either need to get a different type of visa or leave the US. But in general, there's no path to a work visa for most people except an H1-B.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do you think in-person meetings are necessary?
Answer: I've thought a lot about this since remote work became the norm. My conclusion is that in person meetings still have advantages over virtual meetings. This annoys me because I generally love remote work and wish it were unequivocally good. But there are still a few important things missing from remote meetings. Conversational turn-taking is awful online. “No you go.” We can't see the subtle intake of breath and facial cues that signal someone wants to talk or the eye and body movements that show who they're talking to. Google Meet's “Raise Hand" feature is a solid attempt to fix this problem, one that arguably will help shy people participate even better than in person, but it's still a much less effective way of communicating than humans' natural body language. Whiteboarding is still impossible. Nobody seems to have solved that problem yet. Last week I tried to use Google Draw as a live whiteboard. It was okay, but not interactive and not as easy to use as a whiteboard. I predict someone is going to make a lot of money by inventing a virtual whiteboard that's as good as a real one, but it hasn't happened yet. Because there's no need to physically move between meetings, meetings generally both start and end at exactly 30 minute intervals. If your day is full of meetings like mine is, that means there's no time to pee. This is a serious issue, people. It can be hard to avoid distractions. You can't just turn your computer off, and looking at a different window on your screen is a lot less obvious than looking at your laptop during an in person meeting. Overall, though, I think virtual meetings are a big win. You don't have to waste time walking to a room. If the meeting turns out not to be relevant to you, it's easier to leave. It's easier to share and review documents. It's easier to eat and to get up and move around. And, of course, it's easier to wear sweatpants.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How important is an employee’s annual performance review in considering future promotions with their company?
Answer: At Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, the three companies I've worked for, performance reviews had a significant impact on promotions. At Microsoft, if you weren't ranked highly in the past review, that meant that some of your peers were evaluated as performing better than you. Those people are ahead in line for promotion. Usually the people in the top band either got promoted or feel before the minimum time in level to be promoted, so often some people in the second rating band were also promoted.. Google has a performance rating that is officially equivalent to performance at the next level. If you didn't get that rating in the last performance review, it's almost certain that the managers on the team don't consider you ready for the next level. Promotions are done by a committee of (mostly) independent managers that isn't the same group as for performance reviews. The promo committee has access to the ratings and manager statement of support or opposition. At Google, employees can apply for promotion without manager support. They mostly fail but low double digit percentages do succeed. At Salesforce, there isn't an official link between ratings and promotions, as far as I can tell. But promotions are determined by the same group of people that determines the performance rating, so it's highly unlikely that the same group of people is going to change their minds significantly. Of course, ratings and promotions are highly correlated. By far the majority of promotions go to people who were rated highly in the most recently cycle.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why hasn't the thumb print become the universal identifier for all transactions, as portrayed in the movie "Back To The Future 2"?
Answer: In a way, this has already happened. Most of you are probably reading this on your phone. How did you unlock your phone? Almost certainly with your fingerprint or your face. When you go to the Amazon app or Uber or grocery delivery, your credit card or bank info is already there. For websites, your browser probably auto-fills the info. So in effect, your finger or face unlocks payment for many services that would once have required a physical card, check or cash. If you'd like, you can use Apple Pay or Google Pay at many larger brick and mortar businesses, too. But most people prefer credit cards or cash for in person transactions simply because they are very easy to use. If you used your fingers to log in, you'd also have to choose which account to use. The terminal would need some kind of UI. I guess you could use one finger per account, but better hope you never get a paper cut. There is also the major problem that there is no password reset for fingers. If your fingerprint is ever compromised, you're screwed. And, at least in the US, your fingerprint is already compromised if you have ever been arrested (even if never convicted) or in the military. In many states you're also required to submit fingerprints for gun permits and background checks of all kinds, including for all teachers. Almost everyone who visits the US and is not a citizen has had their fingerprints connected for the last several years. These captured fingerprints aren't necessarily enough to log into every kind of fingerprint reader, but it's not a chance most people would want to take. To be honest, I think the real reason fingerprint auth for payments hasn't been more widely adopted is that people immediately think that someone would cut off your finger to get into your bank account. It's a ridiculous idea. If I control your body enough to cut off your finger, I can certainly steal your credit card already. Heck, if you believe I really can and wrong cut off your finger, I can make you do pretty much anything, like call your bank and wire me all your money. And trying to pay for your Big Mac with a severed finger is going to draw some unwanted attention. So the is no real risk that fingerprint auth will lead to increased maiming. But I suspect most people never get past that initial “ick" reaction. I think the reason people don't feel the same way about using a fingerprint to unlock their phone is that most people don't think about the fact that an unlocked phone is equivalent to a credit card. Phones occupy a different mental category from bank accounts.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What do job recruiters just "get" that job seekers just don't?
Answer: We see tons of resumes that say nothing more than, “My name is John and I have had some jobs.” These resumes list a series of companies of no particular distinction, a few standard job titles, and a series of bullet points that state the job duties typical of such a position. From this I can deduce… not very much at all. You might be a rock star. You might be a moron. I have no clue. Your resume looks exactly like 30 others. None of you is getting an interview. The people who get interviews are the ones who stand out. They describe achievements, victories, tangible measurable improvements for their customers. They have passed selective screening processes in college or at large companies. They have published papers, given talks, won awards. They are different. No matter who you are, you've probably got something that makes you different. Figure out what it is and make sure your resume shows it. I'm overstating the case a bit for emphasis. People with undistinguished resumes do get interviews and jobs. They just get them less often and less quickly, from companies with lower standards or a pressing need to hire someone immediately. Also note that “different” has to be a good kind of different. Putting your resume in Comic Sans might be different, but it does not make me want to hire you.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why did Microsoft's Brad Smith back Australia over Google and Facebook? Is it fear or confidence?
Answer: The cynical answer is that Microsoft's business doesn't rely very much on news snippets or links, while its competitors' businesses do. Microsoft can earn both a business advantage and political capital at the same time. It's interesting that Microsoft, via its President, chose to speak up here. They hadn't previously argued for this legislation before Australia proposed it, as far as I can tell. That they are jumping in now smacks of opportunism. Less cynically, Microsoft benefits from an orderly society. Microsoft makes almost all of its money from highly functional democracies, so threats to democracy are threats to their business. They likely do believe that free snippets on Facebook corrode democracy. So what's good for society happens to be good for business and they believe that Australia's law is good for society. To be clear, I think Brad Smith believes what he's saying. It's a common point of view and he's spoken at length about it personally, not through a spokesperson. But I think if it weren't advantageous to his business, he would probably have kept his mouth shut.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is email encryption not widely used?
Answer: Actually, in practice a lot of mail is encrypted end to end. Modern email protocols use encryption, and many people use email directly in the browser which is also an encrypted connection. If you use Gmail and correspond with anyone who's also using Gmail, including all the GSuite business users, your email never leaves Google. Even if the recipient isn't on Gmail, if they're using any kind of modern email server the connection between servers will also usually be encrypted. It's just not very expensive to add encryption, and all of the big tech companies are very focused on security. A couple comments suggested that the question intended to ask about end to end encryption, which would prevent your and the recipients' email provider from reading your email. The problem there is key management: your email encryption keys must be securely and automatically distributed to every device on which you access email, including public computers. This has to work not just for your email provider but for almost all of them, since both participants in an email exchange need to support encryption for the connection to be encrypted. Even if widely implemented, it could still be bypassed by the provider injecting JavaScript into the client side web page. It'd be harder to do mass surveillance, which would be a benefit. Ultimately, though, it would be a lot of work, coordinated across the entire industry, on an issue that most users don't care about. Most people simply aren't worried about Google, or even the government, reading their email.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do hackers "brute force" passwords when most of the time you're only allowed a limited number of tries?
Answer: Other answers stating that attackers don't brute force passwords are incorrect. Brute force attacks are extremely common. Big sites deal with thousands of these attacks every day. Brute force attacks against websites generally take two forms. “Dictionary” attacks try to log in using commonly used passwords like “password1!”. “Credential stuffing” attacks use username:password combinations stolen in previous website breaches, hoping that the victim reused the same username and password on a different site. Lists of these stolen credentials are widely available on the black market. Attackers evade retry limitations by sending the requests from many different machines. These are often compromised end user machines (bots) or virtual servers running on AWS/Azure/GCP created using stolen credentials or credit cards. Dictionary attacks are spread across many accounts at once, rather than hammering one account repeatedly. Another type of brute force attack happens when an attacker has compromised a system and stolen password hashes but not plaintext passwords. The attacker would like to get the plaintext passwords so that they can try using them to log into other systems. The attacker copies the password hashes onto a computer they own, usually in the cloud, and brute forces the passwords there. This attack works by repeatedly hashing passwords from a password dictionary and comparing the hashed passwords to the stolen passwords. Because it happens on computers controlled by the attacker, there are no retry limitations. An attacker who has compromised a low privilege account may also try a brute force against the root password. This only works if the system is poorly configured.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What issues have Google employees faced that is causing them to move towards forming a union in 2021?
Answer: There has always been a group of Google employees inclined towards unionization for ideological reasons, who believe that unions are always a good thing in any context. Workers are always in conflict with managers, and unions are the solution. I knew some of these people personally and have no ill will towards them. On the spectrum of political ideologies it's a pretty benign one. A Google employees union faces some awkward issues. Googlers are paid absurdly well and have incredible benefits. Negotiating better benefits would almost literally mean getting more flavors of La Croix in the kitchen. The biggest danger from working conditions is unhealthy weight gain, or perhaps pulling a muscle at the free gym. So the union organizers have focused on management ethics. Google's managers have given them an easy target. Over the past few years, scandals have included payoffs to sexual harassers, military contracts and censored search in China — all poorly covered up. I'm not really sure how a union helps with this, but it probably won't hurt anything. These issues started some time ago and it's been a while since the last one, but I think the effort to unionize began during the scandals and is only coming to fruition now. The union also wants better treatment for contractors, which is a reasonable thing for a tech workers union to advocate for. This will probably lead to fewer jobs, with the remaining jobs getting better pay and benefits. That is great if you get one of those jobs and not great if you don't. It seems less than a thousand of Google's 120,000 employees have signed up to the union[1]. I'm not really surprised. Most Googlers are keenly aware of how good a deal they are getting and do not want to change that.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why are we not seeing Chinese corporate software companies giants beating Microsoft considering the Chinese enormous population?
Answer: Because of the enormous Chinese population. Chinese companies have a 1.4 billion person home market. In terms of population, that is bigger than Europe and all of the Americas put together. It is the largest one-country economy in the world. A Chinese company can have a billion customers without ever crossing a border. Without dealing with a new set of laws, a new language, a new culture, a potentially hostile government. And there is a legitimate reason foreign governments are hostile: the Chinese government, under Chinese law, has full access to Chinese companies' operations. It's tough for Chinese companies to overcome that issue of trust. As evidence that Chinese companies can succeed without leaving China: Alibaba Cloud is the #4 public cloud provider in the world,[1] almost tied with Google for #3. In China, Alicloud is the undisputed #1. Alibaba is worth $700 billion. They have done very, very well at home in China.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some proactive and reactive ways of countering office politics?
Answer: For a manager, the most important thing is to set the right tone and then back it with action. Tell your team that they should work across organizational boundaries, and then celebrate and reward it when people do. Loop in other teams early. Show your willingness to make sacrifices for the good of the whole. But don't tolerate politics from other teams. Without accusing them of bad faith, call out where you think decisions aren't being made with full information or taking the company's best interest into account. Find win-win solutions. If a conflict results from different teams' top down priorities, escalate. Somewhere in the hierarchy both teams have a shared manager who can resolve the problem. It's not always possible to avoid politics. If the entire organization is political, top to bottom, you aren't going to be able to change it. “A fish rots from the head down,” it is said, although it's a funny saying since I don't think that's actually how fish rot. In any case, if politics is everywhere in your organization, you'll either have to tolerate it or leave.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why are people okay with companies like Google or Facebook taking away their privacy?
Answer: Because it's an exchange. You give up your data and you get an awesome service for no cash cost. Most people find that to be a really good deal. Most people think they don't have much to hide and that it's unlikely their data will be misused anyway. I was once told that only about 1% of the American population shares privacy advocates' beliefs. About 30% of people care somewhat about their privacy, and 70% care almost not at all. However, everyone cares about the privacy of their health and financial data and private messages. I heard this from a privacy expert, but I have no other sources, so take it for what it's worth.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How and when should an employee ask the manager for feedback on how they are doing?
Answer: Whenever possible, until you've talked about it so many times it's boring and there's nothing left to say. Feedback should be part of every 1:1. It's also good to ask for feedback immediately after important meetings, presentations and other big events. When feedback is given quickly, both the manager and employee remember the details, so the feedback can be more specific and better understood. Asking for feedback can be very simple: “How do you think that went?” “What do you think I did well and what could have been better?” “What's one thing I should do differently next time?” Just the fact that you asked is enough to start the conversation. Some managers give only positive feedback to high performers, with nothing to help you grow. When my manager told me everything I was going was great, no areas for growth, I said, “So I'll be promoted at the next opportunity, then?” That forced her to think about where I didn't measure up to the promotion bar and give me that feedback. Although another time I asked that, she said, “Yes, you're going to be promoted.” Then I asked her what I'd need to do to get promoted again.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is big tech like Google and Twitter banning some speech the same as the book burnings in previous times?
Answer: There have been a few different types of book burnings. In many cases, the government or a mob came to your house and took your books by force. Big tech is nothing like that. If you choose not to associate with them, they'll leave you alone. Sometimes people buy books they don't like in order to burn them, as a protest or to take copies out of circulation. On the internet, copies are free. One could argue that removing videos from YouTube, for example, is a form of protest. But usually protests are designed to capture someone's attention and make a point. When you stage a protest you publicize it. Big tech companies are doing the opposite of that: they make it hard even to know why content was taken down or accounts suspended. Twitter has a thing called “shadow bans", where users' posts are hidden from others but the users themselves aren't notified in any way. That's not what you do when you're making a protest. So no, big tech banning some speech is not equivalent to book burning.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is it ethical for tech giants such as Google and Facebook to track and monitor people’s behavior?
Answer: It's definitely ethical for them to track you when you're on their site. They are very clear that they are doing so and you are free to choose not to visit their site. What is more ethically dubious is that they often track you when you're not on their site. Third party sites allow Google and Facebook to track you when those sites use Google Analytics, Facebook advertising or any of several other services. Most users do not realize that by visiting JoesEstore.com they are consenting to send data to Google, and they very well might not consent if given the option. What makes this dubiously ethical instead of outright unethical is that it is hard to get meaningful informed consent. We've all seen those “Accept Cookies” pop-ups required by the EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), but how many people have any idea what it means to click Accept? So in practice, the sites’ default setting will be what's used. Most sites use Google Analytics and its peers mostly to improve the quality of the site, so from their perspective sharing data is a good deal for the user, and therefore sharing is an ethical default setting. And Google and Facebook both believe that their tracking is beneficial to the user by improving the quality of search results and advertising. On the latter, their belief is that better ads are valuable to the user: less annoying and more likely to connect people with products they actually want to buy. So from their perspective tracking is ethical as well. The companies have an ethical duty to safeguard the data they collect. Facebook failed in this duty in the Cambridge Analytica incident. That was unethical. So were their apparent attempts to cover it up. But failure to safeguard data is a different ethical problem than collecting it in the first place.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is something worth knowing that people working at Google know and others don't?
Answer: It takes constant human effort to keep sites like Google and Gmail online. Right now a Google engineer is fixing something that no one will ever know was broken. Some server somewhere is running out of memory, a fiber link has gone down, or a new release has a problem and needs to be rolled back. There are careful procedures, early warnings, and multiple layers of redundancy to ensure that problems never become visible to end users, but. Sometimes problems do become visible but not in a way that an individual user can attribute to the site. A request might not get a prompt response, or any at all, but the user will probably blame the internet or their computer, not the site. Google itself is very rarely glitchy, but services like image search do sometimes have user visible problems. And then of course, very rarely, a giant outage brings down something giant like YouTube or Google Cloud. But if it weren't for an army of very smart, very diligent people, outages would happen much more often.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some cons of working for a large company such as Apple or Google?
Answer: The pros are far more than the cons, but there are some cons. You may be targeted for robbery based on your presumed wealth. You may be targeted by protesters. You will almost certainly be told by someone that your company is evil. You'll constantly be asked to fix any and all computer problems. If you have a social media presence, you'll be asked by strangers. You'll be around so many people who are smarter than you that you'll assume you were hired by mistake and any day your manager is going to realize it. You'll get spoiled by the perks and then when you get another job you're a bit let down. Salesforce has amazing perks by any reasonable measure, but I'll admit that after coming from Google, my first reaction was, “No freshly prepared snacks?” Once you're more senior, your actions have big consequences. You can make the product considerably worse if you don't do a good job. But overall, big tech is mostly a great place to work.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are Google, Apple, and Amazon afraid of regarding Parler?
Answer: Losing their other customers. These are businesses. They exist to make money for their shareholders. Businesses hate controversy. No matter which side you take, some of your potential customers won't like it. Better to avoid that altogether. Parler is very controversial. Give them the boot now and you'll have a couple days of controversy, on your own terms, at a time when most people are going to be on your side, and then it'll be over. Keep them around and you'll find yourself in the news, in a bad way, every time Parler does something newsworthy. The news might even start to be about you, about how Amazon or Google or Apple failed to act. It's an easy choice.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do all engineers eventually become senior engineers, or are only a few people at a company?
Answer: I've worked for Microsoft, Google and Salesforce. At all 3 there was an explicit expectation that an engineer reach at least Senior, 2–3 salary bands above entry level. Both Microsoft and Google relaxed that restriction while I was there to require only one salary band increase plus “continue growth", which was loosely defined and therefore the source of much anxiety for the people in that situation. In practice most managers treated it as a requirement to learn new skills and technologies. At both Microsoft and Google, Senior was the most common level. I'm not sure about Salesforce. My experience has been that all engineers except the very laziest and dullest can reach senior eventually, even if it takes years. It's really hard to spend 15 or 20 years working in a field and not become proficient in something.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How does Google, as an organization, decide what technologies to use when starting a new project?
Answer: Each team will typically have a set of technologies and languages that it usually uses. These are intentionally selected at the beginning of a brand new project to fit the project's needs and/or because the lead developer personally prefers them. Very few teams actually start from scratch, though, so most of the time the language and technology choices are guided by what's been used before. That said, it's very common for a team to build a new component or service that needs a new technology. In those cases, the team will evaluate the available options. The evaluation can range from a rigorous documented process to a 30 minute whiteboard discussion, depending on the team's culture and the importance of the decision. Key factors include compatibility with other tech the team already uses, features, stability, latency, and whether the technology is likely to be well supported in the future. Google as a whole has a list of supported languages (C++, Go, Java and Python) and a huge set of available technology choices. But you aren't actually limited to the supported options — you can generally choose whatever tech you want, with some limits for security purposes. However, the supported languages and technologies have a giant intercompatible and well supported ecosystem, so choosing something else is generally unwise and rare in practice. It would certainly be foolish to build a large scale customer facing system on unsupported tech. I'm sure someone has probably done it, though.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What does it take to become a SVP of Google?
Answer: Exceptional managerial talent and strategic insight coupled with a strong technical skill base. SVPs manage divisions with thousands of people. They are responsible for establishing the culture of that division, which at such a large scale winds up being a big part of the culture of Google as a whole. They set strategies that determine what all those people work on day to day. Those strategies include both business and technical components: what should we build and how should we build it? To get to that point, one must first excel as a lower manager. The prospective SVP needs to build a strong, healthy team culture that attracts and retains top engineers and delivers good business results. There are many ways to do that: some managers are charismatic and personable, some thoughtful and analytical, some are good at asking the right questions and listening to the answers. Google especially emphasizes team culture, compared to somewhere like Amazon that emphasizes results, but you can't make it to SVP without a good dose of both. Technical skills are less important but still necessary. It's impossible to run an engineering team without understanding how the products work and how they're built. However, SVPs aren't there to make technical decisions. Their job is to hire the right people, create a culture that helps them excel, and set a strategy that ensures their efforts achieve the business goal. So it's not critical that they be the best engineer, although it does help. I'm commenting only about SVPs in engineering departments, as that's what my experience is with. However, SVPs manage many different types of worker, not just engineers.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the best career path for an engineer that doesn't want to manage people?
Answer: Most larger tech companies, and all the giant ones, have a complete career path for non-managers, who are formally called Individual Contributors (ICs). There is no difference in pay between managers and ICs at the same level. ICs at higher levels of seniority are expected to have impact at increasingly large scale. The most senior ICs are expected to have influence across the company or the industry as a whole. A senior IC might work on problems like “design the way text styles will be stored in the file format.” A very senior IC might work on problems like “design the Chrome memory manager" or “figure out how to reduce latency 100x.” Not all companies have this track, so you may need to switch jobs when you get to the point that it matters.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Are upcoming tech giants giving China a vital edge in espionage?
Answer: Yes, Chinese tech companies' growing global competitiveness does improve the Chinese government's ability to conduct espionage. It is easy for the producer of software or hardware to embed a vulnerability that would be useful to a spy agency, and it is easier for a government to order such a thing on its own soil. It is also easy for that government to access any data stored locally, provided it's not encrypted by a key held overseas. Under Chinese law the government can read your email — that's not a secret. This is not unique to China. Every government has preferential access to companies operating on its soil, especially companies headquartered there. In practice, the laws, legal systems and geopolitical situations of different countries lead to different outcomes. In the US, the government has to jump through legal hoops to access most data, but they can still do so quite effectively. In Europe it's much harder. In every country I'm aware of, the government can access data like email with the proper judicial approval. It happens hundreds of times a day for routine criminal prosecutions like drug dealing and burglary. It's unclear how often governments actually plant backdoors in software or hardware. In most cases it's probably cheaper to find an existing vulnerability than create a new one. Also, if a government were caught placing vulnerabilities into its companies' products, it would completely badly damage any chance that country's companies might have had at building an overseas market. So I suspect most countries will not directly tamper with code.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is it difficult to get a job for IT people once they have more than 15 years of experience?
Answer: Step 1: Spend 5 years acquiring expertise. Step 2: Spend 5 years cashing in on that expertise. Don't learn anything new. Step 3: Spend 5 years trying not to get fired by playing politics, finding soft managers, or simply trying hard not to be noticed. Step 4: Eventually get fired anyway. Step 5: Try to find a job with skills that are a decade out of date. Fail. Blame anyone but yourself. It doesn't work out this way for everyone, not even for most people. But it happens unfortunately often.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How can one balance marketing and excessive self-promotion?
Answer: Marketing is about presenting a cohesive and positive image that matches your goals and values. You want people to think of you as exemplifying the values that are important to you, to understand how your skills come together into a complete package, and to think of you as highly competent in your field. Your professional social media should tell a consistent story about your skills, interests and values. For example, someone who wants to brand themselves as nerdy might share a photo from a Trek conference or a dorky meme and set their profile photo to a cartoon, while someone trying for a more professional image might post pictures of themselves in a suit giving a speech at a conference, with a posed headshot profile photo. Promotion is about putting yourself in front of people. That could mean posting content, messaging people, and/or attending events. It's not really necessary. I've never done any intentional self-promotion in my career and haven't had trouble building connections. If you are active in your field, you'll naturally meet people, and if you do good work and are a good coworker they'll remember you. That's the best way to promote yourself.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If AI/machines take over low- or no-skilled jobs, what will become of the people who cannot do better than those jobs?
Answer: There are 3 options, which will probably all happen in some combination: This is already the situation today in richer countries where cost of living is high. In Europe, government programs reduce the pain of poverty. In the US, both charity and government play a role, but we're also experiencing large amounts of homelessness in many major cities, and there is a direct connection between poverty and quality of nutrition and health care. It's worth noting that, even today, we could build machines to replace many low skilled workers, but the workers are cheaper than the machines would be. That's in large part because the highly skilled engineers who develop automation are rare and therefore expensive. But eventually the ROI of getting 0.0001% more ad revenue out of Google will fall below the ROI of automating McDonald's, and those low skilled jobs will go away.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the concept of a poverty trap?
Answer: In economics, a poverty trap is a situation where getting out of poverty requires investing more money than a poor person can spare. If getting a good job requires an expensive education, a suit and a car, a person who can't afford those things can't get a good enough job to afford those things. If a person is sick and can't work, but an expensive medication could cure them, they can't work to earn money to afford the medication to be able to work. If a person has no savings and occasionally has to go into debt to pay for emergencies, they rack up interest and get further into debt. A person with savings can handle an emergency without getting into debt or accruing interest. Even if they have the same income, the person with no savings gets poorer and the richer one doesn't. Other answers have discussed government programs that create poverty traps, and that does happen, but it's not necessary. Poverty traps arise any time investment raises income. They are mathematically inevitable.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is it that many believe that the near-term usefulness of AI will come via collaboration, with teams of humans and machines working together, each playing to their strengths?
Answer: Because it's already happened. Do you use Google in your job, or maybe Lexis Nexus (like Google for lawyers) or PubMed (medicine)? That's an AI you're working with. When you buy something on Amazon, a computer tells the human driver where to go, how to get there, and what to do upon arrival. Before that, a computer told warehouse workers how to position items and which ones to put in boxes that a computer picked out and ordered. When you turn on your car, a computer makes sure your engine is working properly and constantly adjusts its operation to match the driver's needs. A separate computer is constantly watching to see whether your car is currently crashing, ready and waiting to deploy your airbags. But you're still the one driving. It's inevitable that things would work this way. Humans do things that humans do best and computers do things that computers do best. Some day computers will replace human labor entirely, but until then we'll work together.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the most in-demand skills in the information security field?
Answer: Cloud. It's not new but cloud has had such sustained growth that cloud experience and qualifications are always in demand. Machine learning and data science. It's often failed to deliver good results in real world applications, but that isn't stopping anyone from continuing to try. Coding and engineering. Security professionals who can code well are so hard to find that many managers don't even put it on the job description. But overall, if you're in information security in any capacity, your skills are in demand whatever they are.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are your views on the Salesforce-Slack deal? How will this impact Microsoft's business?
Answer: Salesforce is raising the stakes, by $27.7 billion, in its ambitious attempt to take away some of Microsoft's enterprise business. Both companies consider their target market to include all enterprise software. Both have strengths in different types of enterprise software, and both are trying to use their own strengths to chip away at the other's. Microsoft is clearly in the lead. It's a $1.6 trillion company while Salesforce is a $220 billion company. Microsoft Windows and Office absolutely dominate the business world, and Azure is #2 in public cloud. Salesforce dominates one segment of the business software market, software that manages companies' relationships with their customers. Salesforce previously acquired Quip, an Office competitor. It seems like Salesforce's strategy here is to attach these productivity products to its core CRM products. The thinking is that Salesforce customers spend all day using Salesforce, so if there are productivity tools right there in Salesforce, it's natural to use those too. They also give Salesforce another bargaining chip in negotiations: buy Salesforce CRM and we'll give you Slack for free. I expect that future acquisitions will continue to extend along this dimension. Because it's so far behind, Salesforce has to play the long game here. But with such a strong core business, they can afford to do so. We'll see in 5–10 years how well it worked. For the record, I have no material non-public information. I found out about this deal the same way you did.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What development programme will you provide to employees in IT staff to promote them into management?
Answer: When an employee tells me they want to become a manager, the first thing I have them do is become a mentor, if they aren't already one. This is something even a fairly junior employee can do. The next step is to lead a small project, where they are deciding what other people will work on. I'll double check everything, because they haven't yet proven they're good at this, but they'll get to make the decisions first. If they made a questionable or poor decision, I'll try to coach them into realizing it using questions: what would happen if X? What do you think Sam will think about that? I'll also ask the person for their opinion on their team's performance and chemistry: how well do you think your teammate is doing on this project? How is everyone getting along? Here also I'll use coaching to help them see anything they're missing. The companies I've worked for have had training courses for aspiring managers, so I always send the person to those. They usually involve an introduction to management fundamentals like coaching and managing poor performance, a review of common management errors like failure to delegate, and a lot of role play. The courses let a person test whether they really want to be a manager and learn the fundamentals early. Lastly, I'll point the person to some books I've found helpful. The person probably won't really retain much from books yet, but they'll know where to look for help later on. That's about as all the preparation possible before someone actually steps into the role. I consider the first year of management to be part of the training program and I try to support the manager accordingly.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What does the typical engineering manager do in a typical day?
Answer: My calendar Wednesday is fairly typical for me. I'll get to my desk around 7:30 am and answer some email. At 8 I have an hour 1:1 with a direct report in India. We'll discuss how his team is doing, the projects he's working on, and maybe his career growth. From 9–10 I have a free hour. I'll answer more email and maybe get the chance to work on planning documents for next year or an executive briefing I'm putting together on our team's new strategy. At 10 I have a meeting with a partner team about roles and responsibilities. 10:30–11:30 is an industry meet up and info sharing session. This is relatively unusual — most days I only meet with Salesforce employees. 11:30–12 is free. I'll use it to get lunch and more email. 12–12:30 is an informational briefing from a partner team about the latest security threats. 12:30–1 is an engineering meeting for a technical infrastructure project I'm not directly involved in but which is very important for my team. I probably won't attend and will use the time to work on email and the planning docs. 1–2:30 I have 3 1:1s. 2:30–3 is a weekly project status meeting for a big project. I'll listen to my partners' status and my team member will present our team's. I may be able to multitask during the first part, if my partners' work is going well, but want to be there in case it isn't and to answer any questions about our own work that need my input. 3–3:30 is a 1:1:1 with my product managers. There's a good chance we'll cancel, which happens about 2/3s of the time. We should probably cancel the series but it acts as a calendar block and sometimes we do have things to talk about. If we do cancel, I'll hopefully get to finish the planning docs. At 3:30 I have a calendar block for the rest of the business day. I'll typically use this to go for a run, but I pulled a hamstring this weekend so maybe I'll work. If so, I'll finish the planning docs and possibly the briefing too. Or, being realistic, I'll probably have to deal with whatever fire came up that day. Around 5:30 I'll stop working to have dinner with my family and play with my kids. At 9 and 9:30 pm, I have two 1:1s with team members in India, direct reports of the manager I spoke with in the morning. My skip level 1:1s only happen monthly, but I usually wind up talking to someone in India 1–2 nights per week. At 10 I'll spend a few minutes organizing my to do list for the next day. If I ran earlier in the day, I might spend 30–60 minutes doing work I didn't do then. Then, finally, bedtime. So in total, I'll work about 10.5 hours and have 6 hours of meetings, 4 of which are 1:1s. For context, I have 6 direct reports and 16 indirect reports.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Does an MBA help you move into engineering management?
Answer: Generally, no. In my experience, engineering managers are hired based on their technical skills, strategic decision-making, mentorship, leadership, and overall ability to get things done through others. The kind of financial and entrepreneurial skills taught in an MBA are not very relevant. Leadership skills are better learned on the job. Also, there is substantial bias against MBAs. The perception is that they are overpaid intellectual lightweights whose only skill is charisma, and that engineers pursue MBAs only when they aren't very good at engineering. An MBA could be useful for an engineer planning to found a company. Otherwise, get a technical Masters degree or just keep working as an engineer. Job experience is the most valuable qualification of all.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is it true that software engineers can't do what security engineers do, but security engineers can do what software engineers do?
Answer: No. While software engineers and security engineers can do a little bit of what the other does, they each have distinct skills. Security engineers spend much of their time on analysis. The specific analysis depends on their niche within security. For example, a detection engineer analyzes log files to find traces of attacks. A product security engineer reviews code and runs specialized tools to find vulnerabilities in software. Software engineers don't know how to do these things. Security engineers are generally weak coders at best, and terrible engineers. They generally know how to write simple scripts, and some know how to build classes and API integrations. Very few are familiar with design patterns or architecture or with less common data structures and algorithms, and most would fail a whiteboard interview badly. There are certainly exceptions, people with both skill sets. As you might expect, they are in high demand.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do buffet restaurants really mean it when they say "All you can eat"?
Answer: A friend of mine looked into buying an all you can eat Mongolian grill franchise. He said that the cost structure is incredibly favorable. You need very little staff, because the food is simple and cooked in bulk and the customers serve themselves. They use the cheapest possible ingredients and are usually located in low rent locations. So even if someone eats a huge amount, the restaurant still makes money. Much more food is wasted at the end of the day than on customer's plates. The biggest business problem is getting customers in the door in the first place.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Are people who switch jobs frequently considered more successful than those who are loyal to an organisation?
Answer: I consider someone successful if they have a track record of achievement, which typically but not always goes with a track record of advancement. I don't particularly care if those achievements came at one company or several, though too frequent transfers are a bad sign that the candidate might be a poor performer or teammate who consistently leaves before they can get fired. I am also skeptical of someone who has only advanced through transfers, never through direct promotion. Some people are good at ramping up and delivering short term results, but create big problems in the long term. I would need to dig into the circumstances of their transfers to understand whether that's the case. Some people just do really well, really quickly, and find that the open job market is more ready to pay full price for the person's skills.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do employers avoid hiring job seekers who have been out of work for a while?
Answer: It's a sign that people you've worked with don't want to hire you. A strong employee with more than a couple years in the industry should have a number of contacts at other companies who could recommend the job seeker. You should also be able to return to past companies you've worked for, if they're big enough to frequently have open positions. Trouble getting hired can also be a sign that your resume doesn't match the positions you're applying for. You might be looking for more senior positions than you're qualified for. Applying for too junior positions can also be a problem, because employers figure you'll leave as soon as something better opens up. Bias certainly comes into play too. After a stretch of unintentional unemployment, recruiters start to think there must be something wrong with you. I don't see this problem with folks who take intentional unemployment, like to travel. In fact, this can be a positive signal, because it shows the person is confident they will be able to get a new job when they want one.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some unforeseen costs of moving your company's computing infrastructure to the cloud?
Answer: Because it's so easy to set things up, your users will use more services and thus spend more money. They may not even realize how much money they're spending. Quota errors can be really expensive. If you set a $100k quota, a rogue project can spend that $100k in a matter of minutes. That is real money that is really gone and you're not getting it back. Businesses have gone bankrupt from quota errors. Security is tricky and not always automatic. You still need to patch your VMs. If you don't, they'll be compromised and used to mine Bitcoin, and there goes your $100k again. Scaling is not as automatic as many people assume. Your site may go down at its peak traffic if you didn't configure things properly - such as running out of quota. Maybe you should set it to $100k after all.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do tech companies often have meetings before 8 AM and after 8 PM? How are people productive in this environment?
Answer: In my career, the only times I've had meetings at those hours was to accommodate another time zone or when there was an urgent security incident. I have meetings tonight from 8:30–10 PST with folks in Hyderabad on IST, 12.5 hours offset. 8 am PST is good for US EST and Europe. Very rarely I've had to schedule a meeting at 8 am to get on the calendar of an executive. I've never scheduled a meeting outside of 8–5 except in those two cases, and if someone in my time zone invited me to a meeting outside of 8–5, I'd decline without hesitation.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How long is it reasonable for your current position to keep you from an internal transfer to a new department?
Answer: In my experience in big tech, a 2–3 week transition is standard, and 4 or more is quite uncommon. I believe that at Microsoft managers were not allowed to hold back internal transfers for more than 4 weeks without special approval.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why isn't it common practice for employers to give 2 weeks notice when terminating employees?
Answer: Except in egregious cases of misconduct, companies generally give months of warning that a person's performance is subpar and may lead to termination. This usually culminates in a formal, written Performance Improvement Plan. A PIP states explicitly what an employee needs to do to avoid termination, that termination may result if those things aren't done, and how long the employee has to do those things, with an explicit date that is usually 30–60 days in the future. At the companies I've worked at, the employee is asked to sign the PIP. So they not only get several weeks of notice, they sign a document stating that they are aware of the exact date on which they will be fired. Companies also often offer a poor performer the option to quit voluntarily in exchange for a specific amount of guaranteed severance. A voluntary resignation agreement avoids a drawn out firing process that's unpleasant for everyone, it helps the company reduce the risk of lawsuits and physical violence, and it gives the person being fired a bunch of money that can hopefully get them through the ensuing period of unemployment.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why aren’t more companies making remote work permanent?
Answer: There is a perception among many managers that productivity has been down since COVID began, although this may not actually be true[1]. I think a lot of companies are hesitant to commit to fully remote work until there's clearer evidence that it doesn't hurt performance. They know other companies will go fully remote, and they'll be able to see how well it works. Going fully remote is a one way street: you can't change your mind and ask all your remote employees to move to headquarters. So there is a strong incentive not to commit to it without more information. On the other hand, it's clear that working remotely is highly desirable to many people, so some employers feel it's worth risking a productivity decrease to be able to hire better people. Companies are also tempted to go fully remote by the huge potential savings on office space. That's why we do see many companies announcing permanent remote work policies

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why did Google, Facebook and Microsoft miss the cloud computing wave initially to Amazon?
Answer: Amazon had a unique factor compared to the others: it had a lot of servers sitting around most of the year, waiting for a giant traffic spike at Christmas. Amazon had a strong incentive to find some way to use those resources during the rest of the year. None of the others had that amount of spare capacity or pressure to find a use for it. I think AWS was also a genuine innovation by Chris Pinkham and Benjamin Black. They came up with the concept right when it became possible. Cloud services would have been created regardless, but maybe not for a couple more years. Edit: Apparently spare capacity was not a significant factor in deciding to build AWS: The myth about how Amazon’s Web service started just won’t die. I had heard it from multiple people who worked for Amazon, but none who were there at the founding of AWS.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do you become a manager if you're a software developer?
Answer: First, be a good software developer. You don't have to be the best but you have to be decent enough to reach the level of seniority where you'll be trusted as a manager. Then, show that you can work through others. Mentor junior team members. Give good feedback. Lead a small team on a project. Lastly, show ownership and leadership. Make a strategic proposal and execute on it. Take on a project that isn't well defined. Sign up to deliver something you don't have total control over. Those are the things I look for when promoting a manager.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why does Google love to develop competing products and services only to shut them down later?
Answer: Google's cultural philosophy is “let a thousand flowers bloom”. The company allows engineers substantial latitude in deciding what to work on, and has a very low bar for what can be released to the public. So it's easy for several people to independently create new messaging apps and develop them all the way to a public release. They will usually all gain some users. But then the company realizes it has multiple versions of the same thing, often incompatible, which is confusing to users and inefficient for a business. So it decides to close the least popular. The users of that service are always quite upset, and rightly so. It's not a great way to treat customers. The recent Google Play Music to YouTube Music transition was much better, though, at least from my perspective. By comparison, at Microsoft when I started there in 2005, a new product would need a proposal approved by an executive, market research, a name that corresponded with the current branding strategy, and more. They did loosen up quite a bit by the time I left in 2016.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How many more companies will follow Amazon's lead allowing employees to work from home past the new year into the summer, June 2021, avoiding the flu season and the 3rd COVID-19 wave?
Answer: Amazon is far from in the lead on work from home policies. Facebook, Twitter and Square have announced permanent work from home. Google, Microsoft, Uber and Salesforce all announced months ago that employees could work from home until the summer - at least. My prediction is that allowing remote work will become “table stakes” for tech employers, that many employees will simply refuse to go back to an office after 18 months of working from home, in large enough numbers that employers will have to cater to them.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is sticking around in the same company for years considered a sign of weakness?
Answer: As long as the person has had career growth, I consider longevity at a company to be a strength. The person performed well enough to continue advancing and never got fired or pushed out. It's very unlikely they're a huge jerk or totally incompetent. And they've shown that they'll stick around for a while, which means I can confidently invest in their development without worrying that they're going to take those skills to a competitor.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Will "cloud computing" last or in 10 years will people move away from the cloud and back in house?
Answer: Cloud computing is here to stay, because of mobile computing. A tiny computer running off of a battery is always going to be less powerful, dollar for dollar, than a computer running in a giant data center powered by the grid. Economies of scale far outweigh diseconomies. But the ability to use remote computers is limited by bandwidth, latency and reliability. You can't use a computer in the cloud if it can't consistently deliver what you need fast enough. Over time, we've seen computing move between servers and clients based on the available network and hardware capabilities and on the needs of users at that time. In the early days of networks, users only needed to send and receive text, so they used powerful servers and simple clients. In the 1980s, graphical interfaces and powerful programs began to exceed the very limited public network capabilities, and most computing moved to desktops. Starting in the 1990s, networking began to improve, and we started to see more computing move to servers. It started with simple text web pages, then progressed rapidly. When mobile devices became widespread, the gap between local and remote computing widened even further, while networking continued to improve. A very fast connection is now available, wirelessly, almost everywhere in the developed world. It's hard to see how new mobile hardware could catch up to remote hardware or how new applications could call for much more bandwidth than is already available. Some applications still call for local computing. Many games and VR need very low latency, which is not yet available, although the recent launch of many cloud gaming services indicates that this limitation is about to be overcome. 8k and 3D video are very demanding of bandwidth, so if hardware costs decrease and those become popular, we'll probably see more local processing of video. Devices like Amazon Echo and Google Home need very low latency for their wake words (Alexa/OK Google) to be usable, so they process those phrases on local hardware. We may see other ML and IoT applications similarly use local hardware. But overall, cloud computing is here to stay.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the basics of starting a big company like Google or Apple?
Answer: You need a few factors to try to become a billion dollar tech company. You need a large total addressable market, ideally something close to “everyone”. For massive profits you need massive scale. You need a defensible competitive position with barriers to entry. You can't make a billion dollars if other companies can copy your idea. A common barrier to entry is a “network effect”, where a product with more users is inherently a better product, so that once one company has a large user base it becomes impossible to challenge. You need a strong team that can build the right technology, manage finances without running out of money, and sell the product to customers. It's common for a startup to be funded mostly based on the past success of its founders. You need to get lucky. You need the right idea with the right execution at the right time, and even then an unexpected event outside your control could still destroy your company. I knew someone whose big product launch happened on September 11, 2001. The business did not succeed. Lastly, you need the desire to keep running your business even after you could sell it for millions. Almost every billion dollar company rejected buyout offers that would have made its founders multimillionaires. It's not very rational from a financial perspective - there's not much you can buy with a billion dollars that you can't buy with $50 million - but something made those founders hang on and stay independent. It might be a belief in the vision of the product, in the future of the company or in the founders themselves. But for whatever reason, those founders held on until the company became truly giant.

Name: David Seidman
Question: I was told I was too nice to become an engineering manager by my colleagues, despite my managers nudging me there, since I care about my teammates. What about being too nice makes someone a better senior engineer than an engineering manager?
Answer: Managers who are too nice don't give good feedback. It's really hard to look someone you like right in the eye and tell them they're doing a bad job, and if they don't improve they're going to be fired. And then to do it if necessary. Managers who are too nice don't give constructive feedback often enough, worried about making the person feel bad. This particularly affects women employees.[1] However, giving tough feedback is a skill that can be learned. Most managers aren't very good at it at first. I wasn't. So it doesn't make sense to reject someone from a management position just because they tend to be nice. There may also be another reason a nice person wouldn't succeed as a manager: if the organization is so toxic and political that nice guys finish last. If that's the case, you probably really are better off as an engineer. And you'd be even better off at a different company.

Name: David Seidman
Question: In a scene reminiscent of "plastics" in The Graduate, a prescient colleague predicted that cloud computing was the future. Would you have predicted then that Amazon, Google and Microsoft would become the dominant players in the space?
Answer: I predicted exactly the opposite when I graduated college in 2005. I thought cloud computing was a temporary trend, and that soon enough we'd switch back to client-side computing. I went to work for Microsoft because I thought that Windows and Office were “real computing” and Google and its peers would go away soon. My reasoning was sound, despite being completely wrong. In the history of computers, we had gone from sharing one big computer to having our own individual computers. Cloud computing was just the latest swing of the pendulum back towards a big shared computer, and it would soon swing back towards individual computers again. Except it didn't. I hadn't foreseen how valuable it would be to pool many people's data, nor did I see how mobile computing (which I did predict) would make centralized computing critically important. Physics makes it much harder to put a supercomputer in your pocket than it was to put one on your desk. I definitely got that one wrong.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Can I get a job working for the NSA as a hacker?
Answer: Yes. It's quite straightforward. Study computer science or IT, focus on computer security, go to the NSA's career website and apply for a job in Computer Network Operations. That's the polite name for what the public calls hacking. They'll even train you: NSA | Development Programs | Intelligence Careers.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do so many engineers in tech have a low opinion of managers?
Answer: Engineers have a low opinion of everyone. Marketing is just a bunch of buzzwords, sales is a bunch of back slappers and HR is full of robots. Accounting is alright - at least they can do math. Also, managers really are pretty bad on average. There's no good way to try management without becoming a manager, so many people become managers and find they don't like it. In many companies, leaving a manager position for an individual contributor (IC) position is seen as a demotion, and may even officially be so, so even managers who hate their job will try to stick with it. Most managers get no training beyond how not to get sued, and many struggle to get good feedback from their direct reports. There are many management situations that are almost always mishandled by new managers, because it's just hard to react properly in a tense moment unless you've been there before. So one reason engineers think most managers are bad at their jobs is because it's true.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some good questions to ask myself to determine if cybersecurity is the right path for me?
Answer: Are you a rule follower or rule breaker? Do you love finding loopholes? Have you gotten in trouble for breaking rules that didn't make sense to you? Security is about breaking things, not building them. You'll never being able to point to something and say, “I made it.” Are you okay with that? When you encounter something you don't know, do you feel compelled to figure it out? Can you often find a way to solve almost any problem? Do you like computers? Do you love learning more about how they work? Or figuring it out for yourself? These questions may help you decide if cyber security is right for you.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What do technology firms like Facebook, Twitter, Google, and Apple need so much money for?
Answer: There are several reasons. Holding cash has tax benefits for a company's American investors. Cash that a company earns and then holds on its books causes its stock price to increase, while paying that cash as a dividend keeps the price unchanged but returns cash to investors. In the former case, the investor decides when to sell the shares, earn the cash and pay the tax, while in the latter case the investor must take the cash and pay the tax now. Since it is generally better to defer tax, companies generally favor capital gains over dividends, on average. Cash lets a company pursue long term investments even in bad economic times. A cash poor company can't invest when today's profits are low. Tech companies make many acquisitions. Cash makes those purchases much easier, logistically. Cash purchases of European companies offer a particular advantage. An American company has to pay corporate income tax on foreign earnings when they are brought back to America. If that cash is used to buy a company, the parent company's market cap goes up by the value of the purchase, and no tax needs to be paid since no cash ever crossed borders. This is particularly attractive in the EU where revenue can be recognized in low tax countries (Ireland), mostly regardless of where it was earned. Tech companies also have the unique position of having high margins with limited investment opportunities. They earn a lot of excess cash, but they don't have much to spend it on. They are limited more by the number of qualified employees than by the cost of hiring them, and they have limited opportunities for capital investments in their core businesses. This is in contrast to companies like Caterpillar or Honda that can profitably spend money on new factories and machinery.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What made you become a "former" as an employee of Google?
Answer: Career advancement, impact and money. At Google I managed part of the detection team. At Salesforce I manage all of it. At Google my title was Security Engineering Manager. At Salesforce it's Senior Director. I don't really care about title myself, and I think it's a bit inflated, but it looks good on the resume. At Google I had 20ish people in my organization. At Salesforce I was supposed to have 30–40, though COVID and a reorg screwed that up. The reason I became a manager is to help people have fulfilling jobs and careers, so having more people in my org makes my work more fulfilling. As head of the detection organization, I have quite a bit more influence than as part of the team. I can set the direction of the team more directly, and I'm more often involved in matters that span the division as a whole. And I won't lie: I got a big raise in the process.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How will Google HR react if they find out that one of their new employees modified a rejection letter from FB to show that he got an offer from FB and negotiated salary?
Answer: I think a person who was caught lying so overtly and materially during the negotiation process would be quickly terminated, at any company. That person couldn't be trusted with anything. Will they forge customer contracts to meet a sales quota? Steal intellectual or even physical property? Inflate expense reports? No reasonable company is going to give an employee a second chance to lie to them.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Since Microsoft is so diverse, does it really have any competition?
Answer: Yes: Amazon and Google. Microsoft, Amazon and Google have tried to enter every major technology market that exists, including: There are a few other markets where Google and Microsoft tussled but Amazon stayed on the sidelines: Of course, Microsoft also faces additional competitors in many of its markets, such as Sony in gaming and Apple in laptops and tablets. In a few enterprise-focused markets like CRM, neither Amazon nor Google compete with Microsoft. But in those markets Microsoft faces other large competitors, like Salesforce. So in every single major market Microsoft competes in, it faces a significant competitor.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Would you rather hire a manager that solves problems, or asks questions that will lead to others seeking the solutions, and why?
Answer: Managers should not solve problems that their team members are capable of solving. That's not their job. A manager's job is to hire great people, help them do their best work, point them in the right strategic direction, and evaluate and compensate them fairly. One of the best ways to help your team members do their best work is to coach them through solving problems on their own. Once you've coached a team member through solving a type of problem, they'll generally be able to solve that problem independently in the future. Your team will get steadily more capable over time, your people will grow their careers, and you'll get better business results. A manager of a very small team (<4 people) will usually both manage people and solve technical problems, because there isn't enough management work to occupy all their time. They should still delegate and coach whenever possible.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How should I answer a job interviewer that asks me for an unwanted long-term commitment?
Answer: Be honest. If they're asking for something unrealistic and they actually expect you to commit to it, they're probably going to ask you for a bunch of other unreasonable things if you go to work there. You don't want to work there. If they're asking for something unrealistic but don't really expect you to agree, then they won't be surprised when you don't. They may even appreciate your honesty. If they're asking for a realistic commitment that you still aren't prepared to make, the right thing to do is to tell them so. Dishonesty is unethical, and I doubt you want to start your new job by lying to your employer. If you agree and then break your commitment, you will have burned your bridges with that company and its managers. You may even find that the commitment you agreed to gets written into your employment offer, and now you've lost any ability to negotiate about it. You may cost yourself the job by being unwilling to agree to a reasonable commitment, so if you're really desperate you might just tell them what they want to hear, but it's unethical and it may come back to bite you.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Are Google interviews harder for international candidates (who will require the company to support their relocation)?
Answer: No. I never knew the citizenship or relocation needs of anyone I interviewed. The one exception is when I'm the hiring manager and was informed that the candidate would need a visa. In these cases, I would have authorized the interviews knowing that if we decided to hire that candidate we would pay for their relocation and visa and take the risk they wouldn't get one. Cost of relocation was never a serious consideration in any hiring decision I've made. It's nominally a factor we account for, but I've never seen it actually sway a decision.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the top qualities hiring managers are looking for in qualified candidates during an in-person interview?
Answer: I look for technical ability suitable to the level and role. That might mean deep and broad knowledge of a variety of security specialties for a senior engineer, or just the basics for a new grad. I look for evidence of good behavior, like teaching others, considering ethics in decisions, or showing empathy. I don't think you can always tell from the interview if the candidate is going to be badly behaved on the job, but sometimes you do get good evidence one way or the other. In managers and senior individual contributors, I look for leadership skills. Can they take ownership of a project and organize others to complete it? Can they resolve personality conflicts? Are they able to think strategically and see the big picture? In managers, I look for management skill. Do they know how to manage a low performer? Do they know how to grow leaders? How do they approach hiring decisions? All of these things are non-negotiable.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some of the social problems you've run into being a part of a remote or distributed team?
Answer: The biggest problem I've noticed since COVID is that there's no good way to do social events with the team.
