Answer: It usually means part of the job to tell senior management (the big bosses) and partner teams how everything is going, and make them happy with it. Opaque phrases in job descriptions are annoying, but then again, I'm not sure what else they could put that would be clearer and not too long.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why should top-level managers carry out regular progress assessments?
Answer: As an employee, if you weren't doing what the boss wanted, wouldn't you want to know as soon as possible? A good manager wants the same thing. Surprises in a performance review are a bad thing for both people. Of course, the manager does also care about how projects are progressing, because other people care about the outcome. Customers might be waiting for a feature before purchasing, or another team might need to use the thing you're making. If the project is not running on time, they need to be kept informed. Also, if there are problems, the manager can often help. Perhaps a team member isn't pulling their weight, another team is being uncooperative, or the team isn't clear about its priorities. These are all things the manager can and should deal with. But if they don't know how well things are progressing, they can't help.

Name: David Seidman
Question: As a software engineer, what are your hobbies other than coding? Sometimes I can hardly find a topic other than IT and it makes harder to communicate with non-IT people.
Answer: My hobbies can be broadly defined as “exercising, especially in the outdoors”. Specifically: I also brew my own beer. Recently I learned to scuba dive, so that may be added to the list as well. I'm planning on picking up windsurfing this summer. Oh, and knitting. A colleague taught me the basics a few months ago, and I've been knitting continuously ever since. I'm still not very good, but I've made a bunch of hats, scarves and mittens that came out well enough to give as Christmas gifts.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do you think Mark Zuckerberg acts the way he does?
Answer: I think he struggles to reconcile genuine belief in Facebook's mission with the unexpected consequences of its success. He seems to truly believe that Facebook is a power for good, as evidenced in these quotes: By giving people the power to share, we're making the world more transparent… There is a huge need and a huge opportunity to get everyone in the world connected, to give everyone a voice and to help transform society for the future. The scale of the technology and infrastructure that must be built is unprecedented, and we believe this is the most important problem we can focus on… When you give everyone a voice and give people power, the system usually ends up in a really good place. So, what we view our role as, is giving people that power.[1] Unfortunately, when you give people power, the system doesn't always end up in a good place. Facebook's problems are now well known: clickbait, toxic interactions, and rampant misinformation. Zuckerberg seems to have struggled for a long time to grasp that his platform has a problem. There is an old saying, “It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on not understanding it.” It must be even more true when something you started in college has changed the world. Furthermore, he probably doesn't have the tools to deal with these problems. Twitter and YouTube haven't figured out what to do about them either, which suggests that they are really hard to solve. So Zuckerberg has a major problem that he can't easily solve which threatens to ruin the legacy of his life's work. I think I'd act a bit strange in his position too.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How many parties does Amazon, Google, Facebook, and Apple throw in a year? Who’s the best? Which celebrities come?
Answer: I can speak to Google and Microsoft. There are no company-wide parties. Really, there couldn't be, because the companies' employees are spread across the globe. My team always had a holiday party, but it was just for that team. No celebrities attended, and nobody really wanted them to. Sometimes they would do a small party at a restaurant or banquet facility, with just my team of about 100. But sometimes they would do a division-wide party. For those, they'd rent all the ballrooms in a big hotel, or a giant warehouse, and fill them with all sorts of food, music and games. At one of them, they had a portrait photographer, and a guy stripped down to his underwear to recreate this shot: At another one, the VP stood at the door and took a photo with everyone who entered, as if it were some kind of special opportunity for us. That was weird.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How can I be an effective manager in a big tech corporation without becoming an emotionless robot? Must I become Bill Lumbergh?
Answer: Quite the opposite: empathy is the best way to be an effective manager. Teams that trust each other get good results.[1] You don't build trust on your team by being a heartless robot. To be a good manager you must listen to your team and watch their interactions, and use your observations to help them overcome conflicts and work together. Empathy will also help you understand each person's values and career objectives, so you can motivate them better. And if you present your strategic vision in a way that aligns with their values, they will believe in it and work hard to achieve it. Do all of that, and I guarantee you'll get a good result. Remember, Bill Lumbergh lost the company millions of dollars and one of his employees burned the building down. Don't be Bill Lumbergh.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is a Google engineer considered the best in the world?
Answer: Right around the time I graduated in 2005, Google was indeed widely considered to have the best engineers in the industry, at least among computer science graduates. It was doing exciting, revolutionary things: indexing all the information on the internet and building the largest, most scalable computer cluster ever, often developing new computer science in the process. Google led the industry in perks, especially free food, and was known for its fun, relaxed culture. In other words, it was a very attractive place to work, so if you had a choice, you'd usually choose Google. And only the best had that choice: Google hired only students from top schools and had a legendarily difficult interview process. It also didn't have much competition. Microsoft was in its unhappy Vista era. Apple didn't make phones. Amazon was a tougher place to work and viewed as less technically interesting. Facebook had just launched. Netflix shipped DVDs in the mail. There were startups, of course, but since it was a few years after the .com crash, those were viewed with skepticism. By 2010, Facebook and Netflix were doing interesting things with data centers, AWS had made Amazon more technically interesting, Microsoft had big successes with Windows 7 and XBox 360, and Apple had launched the iPhone. Google still had great engineers, but now it had a lot more competition for talent. The era of Google as clearly the top company for engineers had ended.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why aren't software engineers afraid that without a union, their salaries will decline and their jobs will go overseas?
Answer: Software has been an important field for over 30 years. During that time, salaries have risen more or less continuously, with occasional bubbles during which substantial numbers of people get very rich. Unemployment in the field is very low, even though companies do send a ton of work overseas. So working in this field means you'll make good money with good job security and have a shot at unbelievable money. So there is very little incentive to form a union.

Name: David Seidman
Question: When will American programmers step up and compete against the Europeans in competition and win a world title?
Answer: As soon as European software companies regularly beat American companies in the marketplace (and probably not even then). Why win gold medals when you can win actual gold?

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do Google, Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft employees have office desk phones or are they supplied with company mobile phones?
Answer: At both Microsoft and Google, the company paid for your cell phone if and only if you had a business need for it. Microsoft was much more strict about what qualified as a business need. When I left Microsoft 4 years ago, they were no longer issuing desk phones as standard equipment. Google did not issue anyone a desk phone except by request. All phones used VOIP, not POTS. Salesforce is like Google: paid cell phone if you need one, no desk phone. There's really no need for a desk phone anymore. A laptop with headset is sufficient. All of us use videoconferencing more or less daily, and our videoconference programs can call traditional phones if needed

Name: David Seidman
Question: If a company wanted to estimate the cost of a data breach or theft of its data how would they go about doing that?
Answer: I recently finished reading a book about this exact subject: How to Measure Anything in Cybersecurity Risk: Douglas W. Hubbard, Richard Seiersen, Daniel E. Geer, Stuart McClure The basic idea is to decompose risks into component parts and evaluate them separately. For example, you might assess the risk that an admin is phished and the risk that compromised admin credentials are then used to steal different kinds of data. You can then estimate the damage from each kind of loss. All of these can be given as ranges or even probability distributions. You can then simply run the numbers, multiplying each set of probabilities by the damage ranges and adding up the result to determine an aggregate dollar value for all of the company's combined risks. I'm oversimplifying the math here - you do need some basic statistics skills to run the numbers correctly. Additionally, practicing estimating one thing turns out to improve your ability to estimate other things. You can practice estimating the number of M&Ms in a jar, and you'll also get better at estimating the risk of a breach. I'm planning to pilot this on my team and see how useful it is. The biggest potential problem I see is that the effort to perform the analysis may be high, and I'm not sure the result will be worth it.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is Microsoft proud to be American while Google pretends that it isn't an American company?
Answer: Microsoft does a huge amount of business with the US government. Google does not. It's as simple as that. Don't let rhetoric fool you. Google and Microsoft didn't become the largest companies in the world by turning away rich customers. Google thinks that it can improve its international image and employee morale by vocally disavowing some government contracts, but the truth is that they didn't have many government contracts to begin with.

Name: David Seidman
Question: You were tasked to hire a team, despite having no prior experience as a manager. What are some specific traits you should look for in the team members?
Answer: Respect is the most crucial. A team member who doesn't treat everyone with respect can destroy the entire team. Willingness and ability to learn are second most important. An inexperienced junior person who learns quickly will not be junior for long. This person will become more and more valuable to the team over time. A senior person who doesn't learn will never be better than the day you hire them. Look for people who get things done - people who build things, close deals, or whatever success looks like in your industry. Plenty of people are all talk and no action. In resumes and interviews, look for and ask about specific tangible accomplishments. Hire for the future. Hire the people your team will need in 6–24 months, not the people it needs today, if those are different. You may need to hire more senior leaders for a team poised to grow, for example. This advice doesn't apply to small startups or other organizations that might cease to exist in the near term. It's tough to be a first time manager building a team from scratch. As a senior manager, I would try not to put someone in this position. You should certainly ask your manager for help and coaching, especially to review hiring decisions. A hiring mistake is hard to undo. If in doubt, don't extend an offer.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Can I change my gender to increase the odds of getting hired?
Answer: I am assuming you are not actually transgender and are merely speculating about a potential loophole. To legally change your gender requires, at minimum, a sworn statement that the new gender is your sincerely held gender identity. It would be a crime to make such a statement dishonestly. Name changes for purpose of deceit are also illegal in every state I'm familiar with. A legal gender or name change isn't required to use a name and clothes typical of another gender during the job application process. The company will also see your legal name and know that you're transgender, as far as they're concerned. They may discriminate against you on this basis - gender identity isn't protected by law at the US federal level, though it is in some states and cities. On the other hand, they can't legally prefer one gender over another. I've been involved in dozens of interviews and hires, and we have never discussed the applicant's gender. We also don't discuss gender identity. In addition to being illegal, these factors are simply not relevant to job performance. So overall, pretending to be transgender won't help your odds of being hired, might hurt them, and could even be illegal.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What will be the long-term consequences of tech corporations (Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, etc.) censoring speech on their platforms?
Answer: At present, censorship is mostly around the margins. The people who get their content taken down are right at the border of policies banning racism, incitement to violence, etc. We also see occasional short term takedowns of content that is controversial but clearly within policy. These aren't really intentional but happen because we haven't yet figured out a good way to review content reported as offensive without sometimes getting it wrong. They're quickly reverted and the bad PR quickly subsides. The net effect is basically nothing. Some people get mad (I'm sure a few will comment on this answer), but the vast majority of Americans don't care. This isn't content they would ever view, and since the cat videos they do watch are never taken down, they don't see censorship as a problem. If censorship ever expanded to content that a significant number of people care about, it would drive those people away from that platform onto its competitors. That's why it will never happen - or if it does, due to a poor business decision, an uncensored competitor will arise. By censorship, I mean taking down content entirely. Sites like YouTube also allow some controversial content but will not show ads on it, so the creators can't make money. This is completely driven by the advertisers, and Google, Facebook etc. have almost no discretion in the matter.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is it acceptable to wear a shirt with a previous job's logo at your current job?
Answer: In my industry, I frequently see people wearing gear from former employers, but only after they've been in the job a while, not ostentatiously, and only if the gear is not from a major competitor. Vintage gear is also okay. People at Microsoft are not going to get mad at you for wearing an Apple IIe T shirt from 1983 (if those even exist).

Name: David Seidman
Question: How can smaller companies attract senior staff?
Answer: Smaller companies can attract good engineers by giving them more responsibility and autonomy than they would get at a bigger company. At Salesforce, I'm responsible for about 3% of the security organization. At a smaller company, I might run 33% of security or even the whole thing. I might be managing the same number of people, but I would be responsible for doing more things and given more discretion in how to do them.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do Mac computers last longer than PCs?
Answer: Most PC purchasers make their decision solely based on price. It's hard to evaluate the quality of a computer, especially if you don't know much about technology. So over time, manufacturers found ways to cut corners. One way they did that was to preinstall dozens of junky apps in exchange for payment from the app vendor. Another way they did it was to use the lowest possible quality electronic components. Even a computer professional can't tell how good the motherboard capacitors are without disassembling the computer. They won't let you do that at Best Buy. As this race to the bottom progressed, mass market PCs got really cheap and really crappy. High quality computers were still available in the business market and as custom builds, but they generally weren't in stores. And what consumer is going to buy a $1500 Dell when there's a $300 one right next to it? But those cheap electronic components, and the PCs made from them, didn't last very long, and people started to realize it. This left an opening for Apple. People knew that Apple made quality products and only quality products. Macs looked like quality products and were sold in luxurious stores. So people started paying a premium to buy Macs in part because they knew a Mac would last. This is why Microsoft launched the Surface. Surface was not expected to sell many units. It was intended to salvage the reputation of PCs as a whole. It turned out to be unexpectedly popular, and has substantially improved the perception of PCs as a quality product. But many people still think of PCs as junk and Macs as quality.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How should I handle being asked to do things that are clearly not part of my job description?
Answer: Ask how you'll be rewarded. The answer may very well be, “You'll get to keep your job.” If so, you'll have to decide whether that's a deal you're okay with or if it's time to look for another job. More likely you'll be told to expect a pay raise and/or promotion in the future. The promised reward may or may not actually happen. Again, if you don't get an actual reward for the extra work, you'll have to decide whether you're going to quit over it. In the best case, they are giving you more responsibility because they think you can handle it and want to promote you. Businesses love good workers, and perhaps they believe you are one.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do big tech companies stay nimble?
Answer: By separating infrastructure from products. Most of the big software companies have converged on the same model: many employees work on shared infrastructure that is not connected directly to any one product. Other employees use that infrastructure to build products. This means that employees working on products have great tools built especially for that company's needs, which speeds up product development a lot. And the company can hire highly skilled, highly specialized and highly paid engineers to build the infrastructure. I've considered only software companies in this article because they are what I know best.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the fundamental differences between impersonation and single sign-on mechanisms?
Answer: Single Sign On: Alice: I want to talk to Bob. Here's my ID. Trusted Trent: Hi Bob, it's me, Trusted Trent, your identity server. This here is Alice. It's really her, I checked her ID. Bob: Thanks Trent, hi Alice. Alice, let me check my books and see what you have access to. Impersonation with SSO: Alice: Hi Trent, it's me, Alice. Here's my ID. Carol here is going to be helping me out, so she can pretend to be me when talking to Bob. Trusted Trent: Okey dokey. Later… Carol: Trent, here's my ID. I want to pretend to be Alice and talk to Bob. Trusted Trent: Hi Bob, it's me, Trusted Trent, your identity server. This here is Alice. Impersonation without SSO: Alice: Hi Bob, it's me, Alice. Here's my ID. Carol here is going to be helping me out, so she can pretend to be me. Bob: Okey dokey. Later… Carol: Hi Bob, it's me, Carol. Here's my ID. I want to pretend to be Alice. Bob: Okay. Hi Alice, what can I do for you?

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are the drawbacks of going into the tech industry?
Answer: You have to get used to change. Everything from the programming languages you use to the major companies in the industry will change multiple times over the course of your career. If you want stable and predictable, tech is probably not for you. You will need to change companies periodically in order to grow your skills and your career. Again, not great if you like stability. Your employment opportunities are heavily concentrated in a handful of dense, diverse coastal cities with liberal politics and high cost of living. You don't have to live in one of them, but your career will suffer if you don't. You'll work with a lot of people who believe their own hype. Engineering is really hard work that simultaneously requires great precision and great creativity. And if it's not natural to you, you'll really struggle. If you work in tech but aren't an engineer (edit: or product manager), you'll be treated like a second class citizen. All that said, the advantages greatly outweigh the disadvantages. But that's the subject of another post.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do companies like Google, Amazon, Facebook, and Microsoft constantly steal each other’s algorithms?
Answer: They do not directly steal algorithms. Attempting to bring intellectual property from one company to another will get you immediately fired. The lawyers make very sure of that. However, any engineer can tell you that it's easier to build something for the second time. The result will often be similar to the original but better. So when an engineer changes companies, the product they build at the second company winds up looking a lot like the product they built at the first. This is well known and accepted in the industry.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why does Jeff Bezos seem to get so much hate on social media in general but Bill Gates and other billionaires don't?
Answer: People seem to have forgotten that Gates was hated in his day too. In 1996 I wrote a story for English class about “Bill Gates' Lonely Funeral”. For almost all of his career with Microsoft he was judged a rapacious and unredeemed capitalist. Today he is known as the world's greatest philanthropist. Right now Bezos seems not to care very much about using his money to better society beyond the scope of his business, and that's why he gets criticized so vocally. We have an expectation that wealthy people use their money to benefit the community, not just themselves. But we don't know what the future holds. Those who criticize Bezos may yet have to regret their words about him as I regret mine about Gates.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What could I do now at age 18 to help me get a job in cyber security/software developer in the future?
Answer: Take all of the math and computer science classes your school offers. Work hard to get the best grades possible, and go to the best university possible. Borrow money if you need to - in these careers, you'll make it back quickly. Learn to code. There are a million sites on the internet to teach you. Which language you learn isn't very important, although C is particularly useful for cyber security because it teaches you how the computer’s memory works. Information about security is also widely available, but there isn't a single place you can go to get it. Write as much code as you can. It doesn't need to be very useful - you can write a calculator or a simple text editor just for practice. The best way to become better at coding is to do a lot of it. Perhaps most important is to understand that you don't need to be an adult to be a great programmer. You can be a great programmer by the time you graduate high school, better than most of the programmers out there, just by working hard at it. You can publish an app to the app store or a website on the internet right now, at age 18, and nobody will know the difference. Good luck!

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you see a job posting on your company’s website for your position, does it mean they are looking to fire you?
Answer: Quite possibly. It's somewhat poor form to post the position before terminating the person, but it definitely happens. If you have other reasons to think they might fire you, I'd recommend getting your resume ready. It's also possible they're looking to hire a second person to do the same job as you. You might as well ask your boss about it. If they're secretly planning to fire you, you can't make the situation any worse, and if they aren't, they'll understand why you're concerned.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you were an L7 at some company, then joined Google, would you retain the L7 position or does Google reduce it based on their equalization policies?
Answer: A senior position at another company will increase your chances of an interview at Google, and the interview panel will ask questions appropriate for that level. A level 7 equivalent at another large tech company will almost certainly get an interview. However, if an offer is made, the level of the offer will depend mostly on the interview results. Google is notorious for offering people lower level positions than the ones they currently hold. People still take the offers, because of pay, perks and prestige, primarily. The assigned level has nothing to do with race, gender or other demographic attributes or efforts to diversify the workforce. Those things are not considered at all in assigning the level.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why don’t tech giants relocate to lower cost of living areas with more affordable housing for their employees?
Answer: There's a chicken and egg problem: companies want to open buildings in places where there are lots of good potential employees, and people want to live in places where there are lots of good potential employers. Companies and people are therefore strongly attracted to places where there are other companies and people in the same industry. The benefit of having lots of options outweighs the high cost of living. This is a good example of the Matthew effect.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you've been a manager + tech leader for a large company, what's the best way to find a similar leadership job elsewhere?
Answer: Job changes for senior managers almost always happen through one's network, usually when a former colleague reaches out with the right job at the right time or when we reach out to former colleagues. When I joined Google from Microsoft, I was interested in Google as a company more than any one position, so I got a referral, then worked with a recruiter to find a good fit. I had many internal references who could speak to my abilities. The recruiter helped connect me to a relevant job, and I ultimately was offered a different one that was a better fit based on my interview results. Next week I'll be leaving Google and joining Salesforce as Senior Director of Threat Detection. I was originally contacted by a former Microsoft co-worker, my future boss, about this role. It was a great fit and a big opportunity to expand my scope and impact i.e. a big promotion. So even though I was very happy at Google, I interviewed for the position. They made me a good offer and I accepted it. Above the director level, jobs often aren't posted at all. Good candidates are contacted directly.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do smaller tech companies survive without being dominated by Big Tech?
Answer: Small tech companies survive because they target markets the bigger companies consider too small or uncertain to bother with. There are many companies providing applications for very specific purposes. For example, I interned for a company that made software to collect and collate data from the sensors in prototype aircraft during testing. This company likely made in the tens of millions of dollars in revenue. At Microsoft I was told that VPs won't even consider a proposal projected to earn less than $100 million, because they already have many proposals worth more than that. Big business is big. There are also ideas that could be big, but probably won't be. There are lots and lots of this kind of idea, far too many for any one company to build or even invest in. Instead, the big companies let startups experiment and then acquire the successful ones.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Does someone who is born and raised in the Silicon Valley have a better chance of landing a job at Facebook, Google, Airbnb, Uber…etc over someone who is international or from out of state?
Answer: Being from the Valley does help in the following ways: Except work authorization, all of these are very minor advantages.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How can I share my ideas with big companies like Google, Microsoft, Facebook?
Answer: Do you want the real answers? There are two and neither is easy. The first option is to become an engineer or product manager with the company. Then develop a prototype within the company. Then convince an executive that your prototype is worth turning into a full product. The second option is to turn your idea into a startup, become successful, and sell your company to the bigger one. Or they might just copy your idea, but hey, the question did say “share”, not “sell”. There is no way to just send them an idea that they will act on. There are over 3.5 billion internet users on the planet and pretty much every one of them has something they think Google needs to know about, and very very few of those ideas are both new and good.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What qualifications must an engineer manager have?
Answer: When hiring or promoting a new engineering manager, I look for: They need at least a little bit of all of these. Some count more than others. For example, previous management success is hugely valuable, and a history of jerk behavior is a hard blocker. The others are required in proportion to the difficulty of the particular management role.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How did David Seidman acquire technical skills to be worthy of getting in Google?
Answer: Getting a job at Google, or any other company, isn't a judgment of your worth. It is only a statement of your qualifications and abilities. My career path was straightforward. I got my undergraduate degree in Computer Science and my Masters in Cognitive Science at Boston University in 2005. I received both degrees simultaneously through a dual degree program. This is a critical part of my story: my entire career was enabled by my CS degree. I had one internship during my junior summer, with a small defense contractor in Pennsylvania. They made me an offer, but it wasn't very good and I didn't like the company so I applied with Microsoft through campus recruiting. I interviewed well enough to get hired as a Program Manager. Over the next 10 years I worked on Office service packs and security updates, then became a security incident responder. After a few years doing that, I was promoted to manage the team. Based on my experience, I was able to get an interview and job offer with Google. I think the key things that helped me make the most of my opportunities were a hunger to learn and the willingness to do unpleasant things. If you consistently expose yourself to challenges and then learn from them, you'll improve rapidly. And someone who willingly signs up for hard assignments is usually popular with everyone.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Wouldn't asking questions give the impression to your superiors that you're not as capable as they think you are and more likely get you fired?
Answer: Good managers know what you should know at your level of experience. If you consistently ask questions about things you aren't yet expected to know, that's a good thing. It demonstrates that you're trying to learn. Even if you occasionally ask a question about something you really should know, that too is expected. Nobody remembers everything perfectly all the time. It is possible to look bad by asking many questions about things you should know. However, in this case, you are probably in a position you're unqualified for. Asking questions is still better than not asking. If you ask questions, you might learn enough to become qualified, but if you don't ask, you won't learn, you won't become qualified and you won't keep your job. It's far more common for employees to ask too few questions than to ask too many.

Name: David Seidman
Question: As a hiring manager, what do you wish recruiters did differently?
Answer: This is something I've experienced while being recruited, but I'm sure my recruiters do it too: when you reach out to me over email, stop trying to get me on the phone. The answer to “Can we set up some time for a quick call?” is “No”. Scheduling a call means finding a free time on my calendar, finding and booking a room for privacy, and spending at least 5–10 minutes talking with you. And half the time it turns out the job is not in your field or even in a different, unattractive city. Learned that one the hard way. On the other hand, occasionally I get an email like: “We have a Senior Security Engineering Manager position with FooCorp, managing 15 people on the WhizBang team, in Seattle. The total compensation range is $200–300k. Are you interested?” It takes me 15 seconds to read that and know roughly whether the position is a fit and worth following up on. And I do usually follow up on positions that seem like a potential growth opportunity - you never know when you'll find a chance for a big promotion.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How does one negotiate time between jobs to travel?
Answer: It's simple. When you are given an offer for a new job, ask for whatever start date you want. They'll either give it to you or propose an alternative. You can then either accept or make another proposal yourself. If time off is very important to you, important enough that you'd decline an offer over it, and you want a lot of it, it's best to mention it to the recruiter up front. Much of the time start dates are pretty flexible, but occasionally they are definitely not.

Name: David Seidman
Question: When it comes to creating safe and beneficial technological innovations, would you have more trust in a united team of government scientists, or the scientists hired by competing corporations, and why?
Answer: If you want safety, rely on government employees. They won't innovate much of anything, so you won't have to worry about whether it's safe. This isn't anti-government snark, it's about incentives. The Director of Safe Innovations isn't going to get fired for not innovating enough, but definitely will be fired for releasing something unsafe. If you want innovation, look to the private market. Humans innovate profusely without needing any encouragement. Competition drives companies to improve their products year after year. But private companies may not prioritize safety as a result of bankruptcy law: in most countries, a failed company's owners can't be held responsible for the company's debts or even its illegal behavior. When a drug company negligently makes a deadly drug and is eventually sued into oblivion, its investors don't have to give back the dividends they received along the way. Heads I win, tails you lose. One possible fix is to end limited liability and let creditors collect a company's debts from it's investors. This would dramatically reduce the amount of risk taken by private industry, as investors demand verifiable assurances of safety. It would also reduce innovation, because the downside of trying something new would now be larger. The balance between safety and innovation would be set by investors - with their own butts on the line. No system can eliminate all risk. Accidents happen and people make mistakes. But the best we can do is to create a system wherein a well resourced group of people has a strong incentive to find the right balance between safety and innovation.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Which companies have become successful or won against their competitors primarily based on superior product rather than superior business model, sales and marketing?
Answer: Google. In the late 90s, Google was one of dozens of search engines and directories. It was not first to market. It was not an immediate leader - that was AltaVista or Yahoo, depending on how you measure.[1] Its core product was outwardly very similar to many competitors. Yet Google did no advertising for itself until 2006.[2] It didn't have to.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Where do you see Google, Amazon, and Microsoft 5 years from now in the military business because of artificial intelligence projects?
Answer: Google has basically given up on trying to win military business, both because of employee pressure and because they weren't doing very well at it anyway. Amazon has substantial contracts with the US government, but it isn't a leader in AI. And… Microsoft just won the massive $10 billion US military contract.[1] Microsoft is also a leader in AI, and has a large consulting arm with lots of experience building custom applications for customers. The importance of this contract can't be overstated. Microsoft makes $33b in annual cloud revenue today,[2] which means that this contract alone will provide 3% of their cloud revenue (the $10b is over 10 years). The contract is worth about 0.5% of the entire cloud computing market![3] They will also be able to sell some of the tech they build for the US to other US allies. So Microsoft is clearly going to lead the use of AI in military applications.

Name: David Seidman
Question: I was asked this question at a job interview: “Suppose we hire you and your first job is to fire 20% of people in your department. How do you find out who's doing nothing?” How would you decide who to fire?
Answer: First, I would question why they're hiring someone to do the firing rather than doing it themselves. It might be okay, if the intention is to rebuild a broken organization from scratch, or it might indicate management that won't accept responsibility. I would also be worried about the team's future, and the company's. That said, I'd try to fire the 20% who are performing worst. Usually it's pretty easy to know who the underperformers are. You can look at previous performance reviews, though they can be unreliable. You can look at the projects people are working on, the speed of progress and the quality of output. Any experienced engineering manager should be able to evaluate from scratch how well someone is doing based solely on their work and the way they interact with their teammates. I would have to ignore peer reviews, lest I create a backstabbing culture. However, if I had enough time to judge through observation how the team members view each other, I would take that into account. Even if I think they're wrong, if the team thinks I fired the wrong person, team chemistry will be badly damaged. Generally, though, team members know very well who is performing badly. I also would not consider the impact on the individuals’ personal lives. If you didn't work hard enough to make the cut, that's on you, not me.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Google unpatriotic and un-American despite being a US company?
Answer: No company is patriotic because it wants to be. Companies act patriotically because their business requires it. Defense contractors need to support the government they sell to. “100% Made in America” is a good sales pitch. Appearing unpatriotic can attract negative press and unwanted political attention. But it's all business. Google is a global company that doesn't do much business with the US government. Its only significant reason to display patriotism is to avoid negative press and politics. However, in today's bitterly partisan America, there is no good press or politics: no matter what you do, half the country hates you. Your best hope is to stay out of the news as much as possible. Google has not done a great job of that. But it's not because they're any less patriotic than any other business.

Name: David Seidman
Question: With the increasing concern of data privacy, how will the government regulation affect the tech companies' profitability from data collection like Google, Facebook, Amazon, Yahoo, Apple and so on?
Answer: The EU already has very strict privacy laws. The tech companies try hard to comply with them. The cost to do so is probably in the tens to hundreds of millions of dollars. Occasionally they fail to comply and are fined millions or low billions of dollars. Even the largest fines represent only a few percentage points of profits. It just doesn't matter. Let's say even more strict laws are passed, and tech companies can no longer store tracking information about you at all, except what's needed to provide their core service. This would impact both profitability and prices for Google and Facebook but not Apple or Amazon. Google search and advertising would be less effective, which raises advertisers’ costs, which decreases their spending. Realistically, this is unlikely to take Google to the point where it starts charging for search. The money would come from investors' pockets. However, secondary products like Gmail and Maps might start charging. They currently earn Google money by bringing people to the search engine, but could easily switch to a direct pay model. If the revenue per search decreases enough, the paid model might become more compelling To the extent that Google faces competition to those products, its competitors would have similar problems. So you might have to pay for GMail and Maps. Facebook has all the same problems as Google, and it lacks secondary lines of business that it can charge for. WhatsApp could charge a fee, but there are many alternative free messaging apps, which really limits how much they can charge. Amazon mostly tracks you while you're on their site, doing the shopping you came there to do. It's difficult to imagine any law banning that. Apple doesn't rely significantly on tracking. It wouldn't be an issue for them.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is it really easier to get into top-tier software companies as a new graduate than as an experienced engineer?
Answer: In my experience, for any individual, your best chance at joining a top company is right out of college. That's not because companies prefer college students. I would take a great senior engineer over a junior 80% of the time, with 20% reserved for junior engineers in order to create a pipeline. The problem for prospective employees is that the workplace is much less fair than college. In college, there is a relatively fair, objective standard for grades, and you'll have many different professors so it doesn't much matter if one of them doesn't like you. If you are smart and hard working, you can get good enough grades to get an interview. On the other hand, in the workplace, if you get a bad project, a bad boss, or a bad company, you're kind of screwed. If your work isn't being evaluated fairly, it may not matter how good a job you do. Your resume may actually be worse than it was out of college, because you'll have a few years of work with nothing good to show for it.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Generally speaking, is Human Resources more a defender of the status quo or an employee advocate? Why?
Answer: HR is not an employee advocate. They are arbiters, not advocates. Their job is to ensure the best outcome for the company. That means following a systematic and therefore legally defensible process that aligns with industry norms. The process weighs the available evidence and the risks to the company of every option. Doing nothing in response to an employee concern could lead to a lawsuit or negative PR, but firing an employee without good evidence could also lead to a lawsuit. And HR people are humans too - they want justice to be served. Much of HR has nothing to do with employee concerns. Recruiting, training, and advising managers are also duties of HR, for example.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do recruiters find underrepresented minority (URM) candidates for job roles?
Answer: The standard ways are attending conferences and networking with organizations aimed at those groups. Those don't really work all that well, in my opinion, because the people who participate in this things are already likely to apply. A newer approach that seems to be working is waiting to get a certain number of resumes, then picking the best candidate, rather than picking the first candidate that meets the minimum qualifications. As a simple matter of statistics, this means you're more likely to get the best candidate who's on the market and also to consider more minority candidates. If there are fewer minority candidates but they're just as good, by collecting more resumes, you're more likely to find a minority candidate who is also the best candidate. And if the best candidate isn't a minority candidate, that's fine too.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you had the choice to hire a person from Harvard with a 3.5 GPA or a person from a state school with a 4.0 GPA, who would you hire?
Answer: Assuming this is a new grad who majored in Computer Science, I'd strongly prefer the state school grad. 4.0 requires consistent perfection. It's guaranteed that that person has a great work ethic and at least decent intelligence. On the other hand, Harvard has significant grade inflation, so a 3.5 is only a mediocre GPA. Getting into Harvard demonstrates good intelligence and that the kid once worked hard. But I knew many students at Dartmouth who had only worked hard in high school because their parents pushed them. They had no strong work ethic of their own. The 3.5 Harvard grad could be a great hire. But I'm confident the state school kid would be.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If managers at Google and Facebook are expected to design and code, how do they give space for tech leads to operate?
Answer: Generally, managers will design and code in cooperation with their TL. This might mean dividing up a project into parts, or even having the TL assign work to the manager. The manager might also make smaller contributions like fixing bugs. Or the manager might contribute to a different project altogether as part of a 20% project. There is also a role called “Tech Lead Manager” or TLM, which is a combination TL and manager. And it’s not uncommon to have multiple TLs on the same project, if it’s a big and complicated one.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is chocolate from the USA considered good in Europe?
Answer: I was very surprised when a Dutch coworker living in the US told me how much he loved American chocolate. I asked him if he really thought Hershey's was good. He said, “No, America's mass market chocolate is awful, but that's not what I like. There are many small chocolate makers of very high quality, like Fran's and Theo, which make interesting chocolates, like smoked salt, that aren't found in Europe.” These small chocolatiers may not even distribute to all of the US, let alone Europe. So perhaps the reason Europeans seem to dislike American chocolate is that we keep the good stuff all for ourselves.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If you have stopped at a red light and it doesn’t change, how long do you wait before you go anyway? If you are a police officer, would you ticket someone who claimed to have been stuck at a light for a long time and proceeded when it was safe?
Answer: This is actually a common issue for cyclists. Some older traffic lights don't detect bicycles and never give you a green light. We've been told by the local Washington traffic authorities that if the light goes through a full cycle without giving you a green, it's considered a defective light, and you may proceed through the intersection when safe.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What was the deepest internet rabbit hole you fell into? Where did you start and where did you end up?
Answer: Quora. I'm not sure how I stumbled on this site, but like you, I found some interesting content and kept reading it. I read about all sorts of subjects, from tech to tanks. One day I saw a post about my employer, Microsoft, that was clearly wrong. I decided to set the record straight and wrote my own answer. Quora's robots decided this meant I wanted to see more articles about Microsoft. Some of those also lacked good answers, so I wrote my own. As my answers got more views and votes, I wrote more and more. 3 years later, I've written 3377 answers. I try to write about 3 a day on average. I'm not sure I'll ever escape this rabbit hole, and I don't think I want to.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What are some psychological tricks used by Google?
Answer: In the early days of Google, the speed of returning search results was an important point of competition. Google was very fast, but ISPs were often slow, so frequently Google's results wouldn't reach the user quickly. To make it clear who was to blame, Google started displaying the amount of time it took for Google to return the results. If the page said 200ms but it actually took 2s, users got mad at their ISP, not at Google.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do technology companies like Google, Amazon, and Facebook all use Linux instead of Windows to intentionally avoid being clients of Microsoft?
Answer: No. The most common laptop choice at Google is Mac, and Apple is certainly a competitor just like Microsoft. People in finance and other jobs that need Windows software use Windows. Developers at these companies use Linux because the production environment uses Linux and Linux is great for development.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why does software innovation at large companies like Google and Facebook seem to take so long compared to smaller startups?
Answer: As an experiment, for a few hours I observed everything I used and noted things that weren't widely available 10 years ago. I also noted any infrastructure I knew to be associated with each thing. Here are the things I used: I also took a look at the most used apps on my phone that are new and innovative. There were only two not already mentioned: In total, there are 5 products by startups and 9 products by 5 big companies. So at least in my life, the question’s premise is false.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Who is the most accomplished person in your family tree?
Answer: Abraham Lincoln is my distant cousin many times removed. My grandfather's patrilineal line traces back to one of two brothers who came to America together. The other's line led to Abraham Lincoln's. So that one's settled.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How long would it take to work your way up to become a principal engineer at a big tech company?
Answer: The Principal title isn't used uniformly across the industry, but I'll assume it means the level after Senior. At Google this would be level 6, at Microsoft levels 65–67. A very exceptional college grad might start at Google level 4. A promotion to level 5, Senior, might be possible within 1.5 years. A promotion to level 6 might be possible 2 years later, 3.5 years total. The two limitations on growth are that the employee will not immediately be trusted to run higher level projects, and promotion requires demonstrating sustained performance at the next level. This speed of growth would only be possible for an absolute genius with an incredible work ethic and great social skills. I have never seen anyone get to level 6 anywhere close to this speed. A more typical path is to enter at level 3 and get promoted to L4 after 1–2 years. The promotion from 4 to 5 might take 1.5–5 years, although some people never reach level 5. The promotion from 5 to 6 can happen in 3 years, or, for many people, it never happens. So a typical path to Principal might take about 10 years. That is exactly what it took me: I left Microsoft for Google after 10 years and was promoted to Principal in the transfer.

Question: Why would someone want to work for Google in 2020?

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is a "purple team" in cybersecurity?
Answer: It's the new hotness in cybersecurity! Traditionally, the blue team detected and responded to attacks. The red team conducted the attacks, in order to identify weaknesses and help the blue team practice. A purple team is a coordinated effort between the blue and red teams. Traditionally, the red team attacked whatever and however they felt like, perhaps loosely constrained by rules of engagement or a specific assigned target. This was often unhelpful to the blue team: there's no point in red team exploiting a bug that you already knew about and were planning to fix. And for the red team, it was unsatisfying to pull off an attack, then be told that the blue team doesn't care. In a purple team, red and blue work together to select targets and techniques. Red team might propose an attack against a target, but blue suggests another target that they think needs more testing. Blue team might ask red to try to use Flash exploits, because blue has new detection techniques for Flash that they want to test out. Red team can still do whatever they want, but they know what will make their work the most useful. Typically most of the blue team will not be involved with the purple team and will not know anything about what attacks red team is planning. This avoids “cheating” by looking for that specific attack more than normal. We have a purple team program at Google. It's great. It has worked exactly as advertised. And it costs very little to implement. If you work in infosec and your organization has red and blue teams, you should make a purple team ASAP.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How is Microsoft able to consistently rally and compete with younger tech giants in cloud computing and software even though it's known to pay software engineers less than Google and Facebook?
Answer: Microsoft doesn't underpay the market by much, if at all. Their offers are competitive and people who have multiple offers choose Microsoft over peer companies all the time. It helps that Washington has no state income tax. Microsoft has an incredible set of products to work on. It has the most popular desktop OS. It has the #2 cloud, and it's growing fast. It has XBox. It has Office. It has Visual Studio and .Net. It has Microsoft Research. It has a top tier security team. It has LinkedIn and GitHub. So there are a lot of cool jobs. Microsoft also has an inspirational CEO. Many people find Satya Nadella to be a good reason to work for Microsoft. I had a couple of personal experiences with him and came away very impressed, and would consider him a reason to return. Microsoft has a more professional culture than Google and Facebook. It is clear that you are an employee and your job is your primary responsibility. Your free speech is secondary to that, so domestic politics stays out of the workplace, and employees have more limited ability to protest projects they don't like. Microsoft also, quietly, contributes a ton of money to charity.[1] It's most notable for matching volunteer hours with $25 per hour to the organization. This is a substantial attraction for some employees. The suburban Seattle location is attractive too. You can live near a major city yet still afford a house and have a reasonable commute. The campus is very nice, too. So there are lots of reasons why people choose Microsoft over newer companies.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do so many of the software engineers working at Google and answering questions on Quora appear so smug?
Answer: Because getting your answers viewed on Quora requires it. Quora shows only the first few lines of your answer at first. If the reader clicks to read more, that's a “view”. A person who views may also upvote. An answer that gets views and upvotes is shown to more people, which generates more views and upvotes. An answer that doesn't get views at first doesn't even get shown to more people. So if you want your answers to get read, you need to get those initial views, and that means you have to get people to click “Read More” within about 2 sentences. That requires a good hook. And when writing a hook, confidence is required. People don't read answers that start with, “There are a lot of factors to consider.” Or, “I'm not sure.” They want to see a confident statement, like the one that this answer began with. You clicked Read More, right? Then once you've gotten the click, you want to get the upvote, and the dynamic is the same. Now that they're reading the whole thing, you can invoice nuance and include both sides of an argument. But you still need to come to a strong conclusion, and a strong conclusion requires asserting that one's opinion is correct. Wishy-washy answers don't get upvoted, and answers that don't get upvoted don't get read. It's a bit frustrating, because I know I come off as a bit arrogant on here, but it's difficult to avoid given the dynamics of the algorithm.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is the biggest mistake made by Google?
Answer: Undoubtedly, Google's biggest mistake was its failed social media strategy. Google’s first entry into social media was Orkut, launched in 2004, which was the side project of a single developer and not part of any holistic social strategy. Orkut managed to gain solid traction in India and especially Brazil, apparently just by being an early entrant to those markets. However, Orkut never gained traction globally. It didn't have much to differentiate it from other social networks. It was never really invested in by Google, perhaps because of its origin as a side project. Google's first strategic entry into the social media market was Google Wave[1]. Wave merged several different kinds of communication, like email, IM and social media, into a single application. Wave never left the experimental phase. It was a promising concept that never had the chance to realize its potential. Instead, it was replaced by Google Buzz. Buzz turned your Gmail contact list into a social network, so that Google didn't have to get you to sign up separately - an attempt to achieve a critical mass of users instantly. However, in doing so, it exposed every user's contacts to all of their other contacts. This was a big problem for clients of prostitutes and domestic violence shelters. Google was immediately sued and forced to settle with the FTC. Buzz was discontinued 18 months after launch. Buzz was succeeded by Google+. G+ was similar to Facebook, with a few extra features. Google+ also failed. For one explanation why, from someone who worked on the product, see Why Google+ Failed. The place looked like a ghost town. For bonus points, the Plus team used internal politics and financial incentives to force other Google products to integrate with it, even when that didn't make sense. Many Google employees are still bitter about it. Google eventually shuttered Google+ without a replacement. Three strikes and Google is out of social media.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Would you take a pay cut to leave a toxic workplace?
Answer: Absolutely. You spend 40+ hours per week at your job. That's one out of every three hours you're awake. Do you really want to spend one third of your life being miserable? If you can afford to take the pay cut, do it and don't think twice.

Name: David Seidman
Question: If someone you have problems with is about to be hired at your place of work, can you request the manager to reject their application if you explain the situation?
Answer: At Google, internal references are a formal part of the process. You will be asked to comment on anyone who says they know you or whose resume indicates that you were at the same company or college at the save time. References are very influential. A single negative reference can block employment, if it is from someone who knows the person well, it is recent, and it is very negative. On the other hand, a negative reference from someone who barely knew the person 5 years ago won't have much impact. Alignment between the reference and the interviews also matters. If an interviewer said the candidate was rude, and the referral says the same thing, that's a bigger problem than if they don't match.

Name: David Seidman
Question: As an engineer, you are tasked with 'breaking the internet'. How would you go about it?
Answer: This should be fun! The way I'd do it is BGP hijacking. BGP is the way that ISPs communicate with each other to know which IP addresses each ISP controls. Unfortunately BGP was designed without security, so any ISP can claim to own any IP addresses. A malicious BGP router can claim to own all the IP addresses, and everyone who trusts it will route all traffic to that network (I'm skipping some technical detail here). Since that network can't actually handle the traffic, it gets dropped. We would have to hack at least one ISP first, probably several, to take over their BGP systems. That[1] should[2] be[3] easy.[4] So, steps to break the internet: In reality, you probably wouldn't bring down 100% of the internet, and your attack would be reversed quickly. But it would be fun while it lasted.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What can end the monopoly of today's technology giants?
Answer: Google: People change the way they use devices such that display ads are no longer very profitable. This might happen if voice or VR become really popular, for example. Facebook: Will decay on its own if they don't figure out how to solve issues of misinformation and toxic interactions. Might also be displaced by widespread use of technology like VR, which would change the way people interact with each other over the internet (think Ready Player One). Microsoft Windows: Unlikely to be displaced from the workplace, but has already lost monopoly pricing power because so much work is now done on mobile devices. Chromebooks are also a dark horse threat: they are not too far from being a viable alternative for small to medium size businesses. Microsoft Office: Faces no competitive threats, nor does any anticipated technology threaten to make it irrelevant or obsolete. Even if Chromebooks take away the low end of the market, it won't matter much, because Microsoft makes most of its Office profits from large businesses. I honestly have no idea what could break Microsoft's Office monopoly. Amazon retail: Not actually a monopoly. Controls only 37.7% of e-commerce.[1] Faces giant competitors like Walmart and Target. Amazon Web Services: Not actually a monopoly. Controls only 47.8% of the market.[2] Faces giant competitors like Microsoft and Google. Apple: Not actually a monopoly. Controls only 15.8% of the global market[3] and 41.9% of the US market.[4] Faces strong competitors like Samsung, LG and Google.

Question: What are the most impressive feats by women scientists?
Answer: Ada Lovelace wrote the first computer program ever - on a computer that didn't exist yet (it was only a design). When later tested, her program worked and had only one bug, which may have been a typesetting error. Answer: Because the smartest, best qualified Indians are the ones most able to move to the United States and other countries. Immigrants in general tend to be more successful than native citizens of the country they moved to.

Question: What programming languages do I need to land a job at Google in the 2020s, and why?
Answer: Google doesn't much care what language you know. It's expected that you'll occasionally learn new languages, including right away. That said, Google's most common languages are C++, Java, Golang and Python, with Python somewhat on the way out, and JavaScript/Typescript on the front end. If you need to pick something to learn and Google is your preferred employer, pick one of those. But it really doesn't matter very much.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do employers always give external candidates higher salaries than if they promoted someone internal for the position?
Answer: Changing jobs has some risks. Your new boss might be mean, the job you were promised might not be what you get, and you'll have to deal with things like changing insurance providers. Most people prefer to avoid change. So employers need to pay external candidates more to overcome that resistance. In my experience, external candidates who negotiate a high salary tend to get smaller raises thereafter, and within a couple years are getting paid the same as an equivalent employee who didn't transfer. I also saw one case where a person negotiated themselves into too high a level and was let go, even though their performance would have been okay at a lower level.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Are we hearing more warnings about breached online passwords than we did in earlier years?
Answer: Yes, for two reasons. #1: The European Union and all 50 US states passed laws requiring companies to disclose when they had been breached. Previously, a company could get hacked and not tell you about it! #2: As more and more high profile incidents occurred, and as executives worried about their regulatory obligations, they invested more in security. When you invest in security, you're more likely to find compromises when they happen - or if they've already happened. So companies are now more likely to find a breach and much more likely to report it to the public when they do.

Question: Do the CEOs of fortune 500 companies have body guards for their security?
Answer: Yes. My former krav maga instructor used to work as one. Often the bodyguards, also known as “executive protection", are paid for by the company, because the company's stock would lose a ton of value if the executive were assassinated.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why did Google delete the account of Jordan Peterson?
Answer: It appears that the question is referencing a 2018 incident in which Google briefly locked the account of Jordon Peterson.[1] When an account is locked, its content stays live but new content can't be posted. It appears the account was unlocked almost immediately thereafter. I don't know anything more about this particular incident than what's been posted in the media. Unfortunately this happens fairly often: a polarizing figure is repeatedly reported by their opponents as violating the terms of service, even though they aren't. Depending on circumstances, the account may be locked automatically or may be reviewed by humans. Even if reviewed by humans, sometimes the reviewers make mistakes. When that happens it's a bad experience for everyone involved. But we haven't been able to come up with better algorithms, nor better humans. It's not just conservatives who have these issues, by the way - they are also common for LGBT YouTubers.[2]

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is the CEO of Google also the CEO of Alphabet?
Answer: With Larry and Sergey stepping aside, the only feasible candidates to run Alphabet were former CEO Eric Schmidt, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, and a handful of other top tech CEOs like Satya Nadella and Marc Benioff. Schmidt is basically retired and the others are happily running their own companies. So Sundar was effectively the only choice. Having promoted Sundar, the Google CEO position could have been eliminated, filled by someone else, or retained by Sundar. Eliminating the position would effectively eliminate the differentiation between Alphabet and Google, defeating the purpose of having separate entities. Filling the position with someone else would have introduced even more change at a time when Google is already in turmoil. Companies often sequence changes like this so they don't happen all at once. I think there are a few good internal candidates, and we may see someone like Susan Wojcicki promoted into the role in the next couple years. But in the meantime, the option that remains is retaining Sundar as Google CEO. So that's what happened.

Question: How big of a security risk is it for someone to upload a photo of themselves on social media that exposes their fingerprints?
Answer: The risk is minimal. Although it is possible to replicate a fingerprint from a photo and use it to unlock a device, it requires a very high resolution photo, a highly skilled operative, and access to your phone or other device that's authenticated with a fingerprint. The type of organizations that might be targeted by this kind of sophisticated attack only use fingerprints in addition to other security technology, and if you're a member of such an organization, you probably know it.

Question: Why does Google have a place to sleep for workers and does it make it hard for employees to disconnect?
Answer: The nap pods are designed for mid-day naps, not overnight sleeping. Sleeping overnight is banned. They actually allow and encourage employees to disconnect during the business day, in order to feel and perform better afterwards.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is the "hack back" bill that is being proposed in Congress a good idea?
Answer: There's a reason the linked article refers to hacking back as “the worst idea in computer security.” It is. Attribution is hard. The defender might hack back at the wrong target. A clever attacker could even attack one organization in a way designed to trick them into “hacking back” at a second victim. Collateral damage is also a problem. Most attacks use a chain of compromised systems to hide the attackers’ tracks. A hack back is likely to damage some of those systems. The attackers will make sure of that. Hack back is vigilante justice for the internet. It sounds good until you're wrongly on the receiving end.

Question: Who wins in the long term, Google or Facebook?

Name: David Seidman
Question: Which type of penetration testing is easier to learn when starting out, internal/external network or website/web application?
Answer: While I haven't worked in either role, I think network penetration testing is easier in the beginning. You can conduct a mediocre test, which someone will still pay good money for, just by running off the shelf tools. Pay your $1000, pass the Offensive Security Certified Professional (OSCP) exam , and you're in business. Application security is a bit harder. The open source tools require a bit more configuration, and it's harder to demonstrate the significance of your findings. I'm not aware of any certifications that offer a one-stop way to start a career. This is just my opinion. Also, some people will find one or the other to come more naturally.

Question: In the recruiting process, do engineering managers at Google also have to solve algorithm and data structure tasks?
Answer: I was asked to solve one fairly simple coding problem. It took half of one interview. I also spent 1.5 interviews answering security technical questions.
