Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Google still an exceptional place to work or has it transformed into just another big corporate environment like Microsoft, Amazon, and IBM?
Answer: Google is still an exceptional place to work. It is also a big corporate environment. We have an internal meme sharing site that is widely used to share company news. We have free gourmet breakfast, lunch and dinner, with a wide variety of options. Our “microkitchens” are stocked with a variety of high end snacks and beverages. Mine also has fresh baked bread daily with an herb butter that varies weekly. My office has a rock climbing wall and a pinball arcade. The only company I'm aware of with comparable benefits is Facebook. At the same time, Google now has 100,000 employees, and that brings some sad but inevitable changes. People in different parts of the company do not coordinate with each other well. Bureaucracy was introduced to try to fix that, which it didn't. Toxic parts of the organization grow unchecked, at least for a while. The company culture has become diluted and bland, though not completely absent. In the 4 years I've been there, the most notable change is the loss of trust. When I started, there were sayings like “Google treats you like an adult” and “Assume good intent”. That is pretty much gone now. It's been death by a thousand cuts, from lack of transparency by executives to leaks by employees to simple failure to execute in Cloud. More than anything, this is what makes Google feel conventional. Still, even diminished from its former amazing culture, Google does many unconventional things and is still a great place to work.

Name: David Seidman
Question: At bigger corporations, do hiring managers and the employees tend to to know the salary of the new hires?
Answer: Hiring managers always know, although we don't always have discretion in how much is offered. Team members generally do not. Sometimes there is a standard starting salary for an entry level position, which typically everyone knows. And sometimes people share their salaries so that whoever's getting paid least can negotiate.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How are software engineering managers evaluated at Google?
Answer: I'm a security engineering manager, not a software engineering manager, but the process is similar. We have a job ladder that describes the expected attributes and impact for our level of seniority. For example, managers at a certain level might be expected to have impact felt across Google, manage managers, or work on very difficult problems. We are expected to achieve significant business results through our team's work. The size of the team is not very important, but a larger, more senior team can have more impact and thus lead to a better review. Our direct reports provide anonymous feedback and complete a survey. The survey score is very important to our performance rating. Our managers also consider our team's chemistry and whether problem behaviors are getting dealt with. Team development also matters. Are we hiring good people? Are our team members growing and getting promoted? This also includes our mentees on other teams. If we have underperformers, are they either improving or getting fired? Improving is best, but firing someone is better than letting them hang on when they aren't meeting expectations. We also get rewarded for contributions to the company and to the community. For example, I started a training program, and a coworker contributes heavily to open source. Managers of small teams may also make hands on technical contributions, and those are evaluated as well. Performance ratings are assigned by our managers but reviewed by a calibration committee as a double check. Overall I find the process to be as fair as any process driven by humans can be. Even when I've felt my assigned rating was incorrect, I respect the process by which it was assigned.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Is Silicon Valley a good place to work?
Answer: Even for highly paid engineers, Silicon Valley is not a great place to work. Even at Google, it's very hard to get people to move there, and many people who live there would like to leave. Companies are mostly expanding elsewhere. The reasons people don't move to the Valley include: People stay because of family, the startup community, the weather, and the cultural benefits of the city of San Francisco.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why is it that some people over 60 or 70 years old are still working? Aren't they capable of living on retirement benefits?
Answer: I had a Lyft driver in Las Vegas who mentioned that he was retired. I asked him why he still drove for Lyft. He said, “Before I started driving, I smoked a lot of weed. This one time, I made this cannabis butter, then used it to make waffles. Each one had about 45mg of THC.” For those who don't know weed: 45mg is an absurd amount. A typical store-bought edible has 5–10mg per dose. He continued, “I ate one of the waffles. It was really good. So I ate a second one. It was still really good so I ate a third one.” That's 135mg, substantially more than an entire pack of edibles from the store. “So after a while I felt like it was time to get in the pool. This was around 9am. My wife came home around 5 and asked me why I was still in the pool. I told her I tried to get out, but my legs didn't work anymore. So 3 days later when I was back to normal, I signed up with Lyft.” So one reason to keep working is that when you don't, you take so much weed that you get stuck in a swimming pool.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How can I start transitioning to agender? I'm not out.
Answer: Agender is the lack of any gender - one is neither a man nor a woman nor anything else - just a person. So “transition” is very individual. It can range from significant surgeries to literally no change. Many people request that they be referred to using gender neutral terms and pronouns, and it's common to adopt either an androgynous appearance or a gender-bending mix of male and female clothes, makeup and accessories. For me, the most significant aspects of transition were: Unlike most binary transgender people I know, but like several agender people I know, I don't really care about having others perceive me in a certain way. I just want to live my life the way I want, without social restrictions based on what's in my pants or constant reminders that people are categorizing me based on it.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do you know someone is actually intelligent and not just faking it?
Answer: There are many kinds of intelligence. A well rounded intelligent person can teach you something about their field of expertise in 5 minutes, regardless of what you currently know. Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, used to ask interview candidates, “Teach me something I don't know.” They may not always be able to do it in person. Some people are not good verbal communicators or are shy. But they can do it in writing. These people do well in whatever field they're in. They tend to be the ones, like Einstein, who we hold up as geniuses, because their intelligence is easily understandable by others. Other people are problem solvers. You can give them a unique challenge and they will solve it quickly and well, sometimes even beautifully. They may not be able to communicate well about it, which can limit their workplace effectiveness, but they do well in fields like academic mathematics or engineering. You can distinguish them from fakers by asking a hard problem and seeing how fast they solve it. Often they will solve problems incidentally, without even thinking about it. Some people are encyclopedias. They have every fact at their fingertips. They may not be great at coming up with solutions or communicating them, but they do really well in complex and fast moving environments where there isn't time to look things up. Great mechanics often have this ability. “On this model car, between 1998 and 2000, the head gasket was made in Cleveland by WidgetCo, and they used grade 101 rubber which is prone to cracking on cold weather.” Ask them anything factual and they'll know the answer. Some people are incredibly creative. They come up with ideas nobody's ever thought of, or they find ways to make things work that everyone else thought was impossible. Examples include comedians and entrepreneurs. You can't really test this kind of person, because creativity is spontaneous, but they should have a track record you can look at. Some people have incredible empathy. They can almost tell you what you're feeling, and they know what to say to connect emotionally with you. They make great managers and therapists. You can't really test this either unless you're emotionally gifted yourself, and if you are, you'll know.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do many security people not know how to program?
Answer: It's not an important part of the job for most roles. Only a small number of people write most of the software and everyone else just uses it. You do need to know a lot about how computers and networks work, and you need to know a little bit of scripting at least. Some companies, including Google, do want security engineers to be coders. But in a tight employment market, security engineers who code are hard to find and expensive, so many companies choose to hire people who can't code. The reason companies like Google hire engineers who code is that their coding skill is more valuable when working at high scale and with an existing infrastructure to build on.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Do Google and other big product companies ask data structures and algorithms problems in their interview if we are applying for a security engineer or any hacker position?
Answer: Google does ask coding problems in most security engineering interviews, in addition to questions about security. The coding questions are similar to the ones used for software engineers, but a security engineer isn't expected to code as well as a software engineer at the same level.

Name: David Seidman
Question: When a company is changing its software’s user interface, how much opinion do the executives of the company have in it?
Answer: When I worked on Microsoft Office, a code change caused the mouse pointer to briefly change to the “waiting” cursor any time you clicked on a new email in Outlook. Bill Gates told Office management, “This is absolutely unacceptable.” It was fixed, but not for several months. When Office changed its UI to the Ribbon, the change was heavily reviewed by executives up to the CEO level on an ongoing basis. However, it was reviewed on the basis of data from focus groups, usability experiments and feedback and telemetry from internal users. Tons of data were collected, and the decision to proceed with the UI was based on this data. Microsoft employees resisted the change internally, so someone put up posters all over campus giving pieces of the data. It was pretty convincing. Please don’t comment about how much you hate the Ribbon interface. You can’t please all the people all the time, but the data showed that most users eventually come to prefer the new interface and that overall happiness with Office is higher. If that’s not you, sorry.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What should a male employee do if their female manager grabs his behind?
Answer: Technically, this is probably sexual assault. It is definitely something to report to HR. Sexual touching, or anything close to it, is not appropriate in the workplace. There is also a risk that the manager will treat the employee worse because she feels the employee didn’t respond to her gesture the way she wanted. This is a pretty mild offense and probably nothing will happen from HR. It’s worth mentioning to the manager that it made you uncomfortable. She may not realize it, since it’s such a small gesture and since women can generally get away with a lot more sexual abuse than a man can. If the genders were reversed, there would be no question that it’s inappropriate.

Name: David Seidman
Question: For someone trying to get into cyber security with no experience, and without attending college, what is the best path to gain enough knowledge to enter the field?
Answer: Get a job at a help desk. Most organizations will promote good performers from help desk to IT; if yours won't, get an IT job somewhere else. In that job, volunteer to take on security-related work like firewall and IDS management. Based on your IT experience, you should be able to get an entry level security job. Optionally, get some security certifications. SANS certifications are the best if your company will pay for them, but too expensive otherwise. OSCP is also good and more affordable. You should also study using online resources related to your chosen niche (forensics, red team, detection, etc.). The ability to teach oneself is highly valued in the industry.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How do people working at tech companies like Facebook and Google feel about their company mining personal data from its users, including their own?
Answer: I don't care. They're going to use this data for two things: Neither of those troubles me at all. Overall it's pretty low on my list of things I worry about the government doing.

Question: How did Microsoft computers go from needing a lot of third party anti-virus software for full protection, to Windows Defender being the only one you need?
Answer: To be clear, antivirus is an antiquated technology. Most antivirus products don't find most modern viruses promptly or at all, because viruses automatically mutate to become undetectable. AV programs are mostly good at finding older and very simple viruses.

Name: David Seidman
Question: Why do the major tech companies like Google and Facebook take it upon themselves to become so involved in politics?
Answer: Actually, they'd really rather be left out of politics, but they don't have a choice. Politics is bad for business. No matter what you do, half the country will hate it. Companies want the support of politicians, to influence policy in their favor, and occasionally they need to use their public voice to shift opinions on matters that are very important to them. But they do not want to be visibly involved in politics if they have a choice. But Facebook and Google don't have a choice. Their products are inherently political. They are forced to make choices with political implications. Some examples: *Pro-Nazi material is in fact illegal in some countries, but not the US. Please don't argue in the comments about which decisions these companies have made. The point is that they have to make a choice, and there will always be many people who wish they had made it differently.

Name: David Seidman
Question: What is more important/valued in today's workplace, strong verbal communication or strong written communication?
Answer: In my experience, in engineering roles at big tech companies, written communication is more important than verbal. Almost everything important is turned into a document at some point, and many important conversations happen over email. At Amazon, meetings start with everyone silently reading a document. At both Microsoft and Google, design docs, user journeys and product roadmaps were the most important work other than actual code. Verbal communication is very important too. Engineers who have trouble explaining their ideas on a whiteboard are less successful. But every important whiteboard session eventually becomes a doc, and many ideas are first shared in written form. I've worked with multiple decent engineers who I would describe as not speaking English. But their writing was okay, and that was enough for them to have a career.

Name: David Seidman
Question: How would you make company meetings less terrible?
Answer: Ask ahead of time, “What is the goal of this meeting?” Keep asking for clarification until you're happy. “Can we do this in email?” Status meetings shouldn't exist, except very short stand-ups. “I don't think I'm needed for this. Please let me know if you disagree.” Not “Am I needed?” - you want to be more firm than that. If a decision is to be made: “Do the people invited to this meeting have the authority to make this decision or submit a recommendation to the decision maker?” Keep time actively: “We have 15 minutes left. We need to stop proposing new ideas and start trying to pick one.” Most of these are things you can do without management support. If the manager is the one that's setting up useless meetings, you may have to word things a bit more gently, but they will probably be open to these points. Managers hate boring meetings too.

Question: Is it rude to ask the recruiter what the budgeted salary range is for a position?
Answer: No, it's reasonable to ask exactly that question. They don't want to waste time on you if you wouldn't take the job anyway. The recruiter won't always tell you, though, especially if they're confident you'd take what they're prepared to offer.
